&#124;  &#124; The root user (only) can customize and add to the jobs that are run automatically at system bootup. Some systems will use the System V method; others (even some SVR4 systems) will use the BSD method. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
|  

&#124; Page 303 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Look in the directory named /etc. If your system has files called rc, rc0, and rc2, and if it has directories called rc.d, rc0.d, and rc2.d, :it is using the System V type system startup programs or scripts. These are called *rc scripts* (rc stands for run control) because these scripts control how you enter or leave certain run levels. (Table 12.1 shows the common System V run levels.) rc2 is a script program that is run when the system changes to run level 2 (multi-user mode). The rc2 script program uses files in directory rc2.d, as in this example from SCO UNIX: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; I01MOUNTFSYS*      P21perf         P90RESERVED*      S85nis* ![arrow.gif](content/4505ed21b36efb4ebf4df5206fc03bad.gif)S91manahttp*
P00SYSINIT*        P70uucp*        P93scohttp*       S85tcp*
![arrow.gif](content/4505ed21b36efb4ebf4df5206fc03bad.gif)S95psleeper*
P03RECOVERY*       P75cron*        P95calserver*     S88edge*
![arrow.gif](content/4505ed21b36efb4ebf4df5206fc03bad.gif)S99apcssd*
P04CLEAN*          P86scologin*    S00MDAC*          S89nfs*
![arrow.gif](content/4505ed21b36efb4ebf4df5206fc03bad.gif)messages/
P05RMTMPFILES*     P86sendmail*    S35dlpi           S90atlas*
P15HWDNLOAD*       P86xdlls*       S60sync*          S90fasttrack*
P16KERNINIT*       P87USRDAEMON*   S80lp*            S90iproute*
P20sysetup*        P88USRDEFINE*   S84rpcinit*       S90secure* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; After the first letter, each script has a number that controls the order in which the scripts will run. Table 12.2 shows what the first letter of each script means: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  

&#124; Table 12.2 System V rc script prefixes. &#124;
&#124; Prefix Letter &#124; Meaning &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124; K &#124; Kills a process by running this script &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124; S &#124; Starts a process by running this script &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124; P &#124; Runs P numbers in parallel if there are no S or K scripts in that range (SCO UNIX only) &#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; For example, in the previous output listing, you can see that the lp spooling system is started first, and then tcp networking, and then nfs. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
|  

&#124; Page 304 &#124;

&#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;  &#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Warning &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;  &#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; This directory should not be modified by beginners. Errors could prevent the system from booting. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Modifying the System V Startup Scripts &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 1\. In this directory, create your own script whose name begins with S99\. This will cause your script to execute after the other initialization scripts. Set the owner, group, and permissions to match the other files in this directory. There can be more than one script that starts with S99. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 2\. In your S99 script, enter the system commands you want to run when the system goes to multi-user mode. Use full pathnames for each command, directory, and file; for example, you would use /etc/shutdown instead of shutdown. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; If in doubt, use the type command to make sure you have the correct full pathname of commands, as in this example: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; # type shutdown shutdown is /sbin/shutdown
# &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 3\. Do not create backup copies of your script in this rc2.d directory. If you do, S99yourscript.bak (for example) would be executed during every bootup along with S99yourscript because both are in /etc/rc2.d. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 4\. Use & to run subtasks in the background in order to prevent the possibility of hanging the system and preventing a reboot; for example, the stty command can be used to set the baud rate of a port, but if the device is not readyif, for example, a modem is waiting for an incoming callthe stty can hang until the device is ready. If this stty command is in your rc script, the system will also hang, and youll have to reset and go to single user mode to correct the problem. To prevent such a problem, create a script that accesses the desired port and call that script from the rc script in the background, as shown here: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; /usr/startup/portsetup & &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 5\. If your function needs to execute some particular code during system startup and some other code when the system is shut down, you should perform this additional step. Put a copy of your script in /etc/init.d using a name that does not begin with S99\. Solaris uses a hard link to do this; SCO &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
|  

&#124; Page 305 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; OpenServer 5 uses complex symbolic links. To find out how to do it on your system, look at other scripts in rc2.d and init.d and follow their examples. The idea is to have one script that handles both the startup and shutdown tasks for this function. The script should save $1 as a mode and then, if that mode is started, the script should execute startup code; when that mode is stopped, the script should execute shutdown code. When you finish, link this script into the multi-user startup directory (/etc/rc2.d) or the shutdown directory (/etc/rc0.d) and add S99 for startup or K## for shutdown. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; *Automating Jobs at System Shutdown on System V UNIX (rc0.d).* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; On System V type systems, there is a directory called /etc/rc0.d that contains scripts similar to those in /etc/rc2.d. You could add your script to rc0.d to run when the system changes to run level 0 (the totally shutdown state). &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Often a better ideaand one that will work in BSD systems alsois to create your own script as described in the following procedure. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;  &#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Note &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;  &#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; This procedure will work on both System V and BSD type systems. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Creating Your Own Script to Invoke Shutdown &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 1\. Enter the command $ type shutdown and press Enter. Youll see output something like this: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; shutdown is /usr/sbin/shutdown          $ &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; This is the full pathname of shutdown. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 2\. Use the cd command to change to the directory that shutdown is in. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 3\. Create a text file and name it shut. (This is not a standard name, and you can choose a different name for this alternative to the shutdown command.) &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Insert the commands you want to run during shutdown. Then end your script with these lines: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; cd /[sr] shutdown OPTS &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
|  

&#124; Page 306 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; replacing *OPTS* with the options needed by shutdown on your system. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 4\. Use the chmod, chown, and chgrp commands to give shut the same permissions, owner, and group as shutdown. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 5\. Now use the shut command instead of shutdown anytime you want to shut down your system. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; SEE ALSO &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; ![sarrow.gif](content/ad91af06ad96c57f0a338bded4c42f0e.gif)*For more information on writing shell scripts, see page 637* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;  &#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Warning &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;  &#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; There is a danger that some administrator or system process will use the shutdown command directly instead of your shut script. If this is a critical issue, add a shutdown script to/etc/rc0.d instead of creating this shut script. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; *Automating Jobs at System Startup on BSD UNIX (rc scripts)* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; If your system uses BSD startup scripts, you will find a number of scripts whose names begin with rc followed by a period, such as rc.net. All these rc scripts will be in the /etc directory. However, not all rc scripts are run during system startup. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; If you run the following command on an AIX UNIX system, &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; ls -lu /etc/rc* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; you will see output similar to this: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; -r-xr-xr--   1 bin      bin         1786 Aug 21 16:03 ![arrow.gif](content/4505ed21b36efb4ebf4df5206fc03bad.gif)/etc/rc
-rw-r--r--   1 root     system        48 Feb  4  1996
![arrow.gif](content/4505ed21b36efb4ebf4df5206fc03bad.gif)/etc/rc.bak
-r-xr-xr--   1 bin      bin         2502 Feb  4  1996
![arrow.gif](content/4505ed21b36efb4ebf4df5206fc03bad.gif)/etc/rc.bsdnet
-r-x------   1 root     system     21187 Feb  4  1996
![arrow.gif](content/4505ed21b36efb4ebf4df5206fc03bad.gif)/etc/rc.motpowerfail
-rw-r--r--   1 root     system       571 Feb  4  1996
![arrow.gif](content/4505ed21b36efb4ebf4df5206fc03bad.gif)/etc/rc.ncs
-r-xr-xr--   1 bin      bin         7352 Aug 21 16:03
![arrow.gif](content/4505ed21b36efb4ebf4df5206fc03bad.gif)/etc/rc.net
-r-xr-xr--   1 bin      bin         4554 Aug 21 16:03
![arrow.gif](content/4505ed21b36efb4ebf4df5206fc03bad.gif)/etc/rc.net.serial
-rw-r--r--   1 root     system       982 Feb  4  1996
![arrow.gif](content/4505ed21b36efb4ebf4df5206fc03bad.gif)/etc/rc.netls
-rwxr-xr-x   1 root     system      4201 Aug 21 16:04
![arrow.gif](content/4505ed21b36efb4ebf4df5206fc03bad.gif)/etc/rc.nfs
-rwx------   1 root     system     29511 Feb  4  1996
![arrow.gif](content/4505ed21b36efb4ebf4df5206fc03bad.gif)/etc/rc.powerfail
-rwxrwxr--   1 root     system      4180 Aug 21 16:04
![arrow.gif](content/4505ed21b36efb4ebf4df5206fc03bad.gif)/etc/rc.tcpip &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
|  

&#124; Page 307 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; The -lu option to ls shows you when the rc scripts were last accessed. You can see that only five of the scripts were used in the last reboot on Aug 21 at 16:04\. The other rc scripts have not been accessed since 1996. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Here are lines from the /etc/inittab file, which executes some of these rc scripts on startup. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; brc::sysinit:/sbin/rc.boot 3 >/dev/console 2>&1 # Phase 3 of ![arrow.gif](content/4505ed21b36efb4ebf4df5206fc03bad.gif)system boot
powerfail::powerfail:/etc/rc.motpowerfail -t 5 2>&1 &#124; alog
![arrow.gif](content/4505ed21b36efb4ebf4df5206fc03bad.gif)-tboot > /dev/console 2>&1 # Power Failure Detection
rc:2:wait:/etc/rc 2>&1 &#124; alog -tboot > /dev/console # Multi-
![arrow.gif](content/4505ed21b36efb4ebf4df5206fc03bad.gif)User checks
...
rctcpip:2:wait:/etc/rc.tcpip > /dev/console 2>&1 # Start
![arrow.gif](content/4505ed21b36efb4ebf4df5206fc03bad.gif)TCP/IP daemons
rcnfs:2:wait:/etc/rc.nfs > /dev/console 2>&1 # Start NFS
![arrow.gif](content/4505ed21b36efb4ebf4df5206fc03bad.gif)Daemons
... &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; To run a job at system startup, you must insert the job within one of the rc scripts that is run at startup. This is a job for an experienced programmer and should not be attempted by a beginner. Errors could prevent your system from booting correctly later. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Automating Jobs by Any User (profile, *cron, at, batch*) &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Regular users can automate particular jobs to run when they log in, or at certain times, or on certain days. The system administrator uses similar mechanisms to run system processes periodically. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; *Automating Jobs When the User Logs In* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Two files are executed by every Bourne or Korn shell user during login: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; /etc/profile &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; .profile (in the users own home directory) &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
|  

&#124; Page 308 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Only the root user can modify /etc/profile because changes in that file affect the logins for all users. For security reasons, you should never give write permission for that file to anyone else. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;  &#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Safety tip: Use two screens when modifying/etc/profile or .profile &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;  &#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; If you make errors when changing these files, you could prevent even the root user from logging back in. After you change/etc/profile or .profile, make sure that you can still log in successfully from another screen. If that fails, you are still logged in on your first screen, and you can correct or undo your change. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Users can usually modify their own .profile files to set up their environment preferences on log in. (On some systems, the administrator might allow users read access to .profile but not write access in order to prevent users from making incorrect or undesirable changes to their .profile files.) Execution of the lines in /etc/profile and .profile has the same effect as if the user typed those same lines at the keyboard just after logging in. For example, an exit command from /etc/profile or .profile will put the user back at the login prompt and force a new login. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; /etc/profile and .profile are good places to set shell variables such as PATH, CDPATH, TERM, and umask. Preferred stty options for the port can be set automatically also. Changes to /etc/profile affect all users, but those changes can be altered by code in .profile in the users home directory. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;  &#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Put df in roots .profile &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;  &#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; The system administrator (root) must constantly monitor all filesystems to make sure they are not filling up because that could cause application errors, system errors, and even file corruption. df shows the disk free blocks. Adding df to roots .profile allows root to see how much disk space is available on each root login. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; /etc/profile can also be used to add extra security to your system. For example, using standard Bourne shell programming, /etc/profile could check to see if a user is logging in from a modem port and if so, only allow login at restricted times or ask for an extra password. If the /etc/profile code executes the exit command, the users login will terminate, and he or she will go back to the initial login prompt. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; *Scheduling Jobs to Re-run Periodically (*cron*)* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; UNIX maintains a set of tables called *crontabs* (chronological tables), that contain jobs scheduled to run periodically. There is one table or file, usually in /usr/spool/cron/crontabs, for each user who has submitted a cron job. The system runs that job using that users account. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; To see if any cron jobs have been submitted and to view them, you use the -l option (list) with the crontab command. If you are logged in as root, you might see output like this: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; # crontab -l  17 5 * * 0 /etc/cleanup > /dev/null &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
|  

&#124; Page 309 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 0 2 * * 0,4 /usr/lib/cron/logchecker 3 3 * * * /usr/lib/cleantmp > /dev/null
1 3 * * * /etc/setclk -rd1800 > /dev/null 2>&1
5 18 * * 1-5 /usr/lib/sa/sa2 -s 8:00 -e 18:01 -i 1200 -A
30 1 * * 2,3,4,5,6 /etc/edge.nightly -MB -n root -d
![arrow.gif](content/4505ed21b36efb4ebf4df5206fc03bad.gif)/dev/null 1>/dev/null 2>&1
5 4 * * 0 /etc/shutdown -g5 -i6 -y
# &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Each line in crontabs has six fields separated by one or more spaces or tabs. Table 12.3 describes the six fields and their contents. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  

&#124; Table 12.3 Fields in crontabs. &#124;
&#124; Field &#124; Function &#124; Possible range of values &#124;  &#124;
&#124; 1 &#124; minute of the hour &#124; 059 &#124;  &#124;
&#124; 2 &#124; hour of the day &#124; 023 &#124;  &#124;
&#124; 3 &#124; day of the month &#124; 131 &#124;  &#124;
&#124; 4 &#124; month of the year &#124; 112 &#124;  &#124;
&#124; 5 &#124; day of the week &#124; 06 (0 refers to Sunday) &#124;  &#124;
&#124; 6 &#124; command to run &#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; You can indicate consecutive ranges with a dash as in 15\. Multiple values in one field can be specified in any order and should be separated by a comma (and no spaces), such as 1,3,7,2,25. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; In Table 12.3, the command to run (in field 6) can be a UNIX command or a shell script. Use a full pathname to reference all files and any commands that are not in /bin or /usr/bin. Any standard output or standard error messages that are not redirected to a file will be mailed to the user who submitted the cron job. If the system was down at the time and day it was scheduled to run the job, that job will be skipped. It will run again at the next scheduled time and day if the system is up then. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
|  

&#124; Page 310 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Adding/Removing/Modifying a Cron Job &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 1\. Log in as the user whose cron job you want to modify. (Dont run cron jobs as root unless it is absolutely necessary.) If you have never added a cron job before, use an account other than root, sys, adm, or uucp so you can practice adding and removing a test cron job first. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 2\. Enter cd to go to your home directory. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 3\. Unless the command to run via cron is extremely simple, use vi or another editor to create a shell script (called a *cron script* for this procedure). In that cron script, insert the desired command(s) you want to run from cron. You should use a cron script whenever you want to run a sequence of multiple commands from cron. Test your cron script by running it directly from your terminal. Use full pathnames within your cron script for any files to be accessed. Use full pathnames for any system commands that are not in /bin or /usr/bin. If you are using cron for the first time, try using only the date command, which will be mailed to you from cron. Another good first cron script is to create a small result file in your home directory or /tmp, the result of which is shown here: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; echo cron test `date` > /tmp/fred.cron.tst &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 4\. At the shell prompt, test your ERASE key as follows. Enter datex but before pressing the Enter key, press the Backspace key or Ctrl+H to erase the x. Then press the Enter key. The current date and time should be displayed. If not, your ERASE key is not working; do not proceed further. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 5\. Next, enter this command slowly and carefully: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; crontab -l > cronfile &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Check your command carefully before you press the Enter key. Use your ERASE key slowly and carefully to correct any errors. If you get an error saying either No such file or Can't open file, you have no current cron jobs. Just ignore this error and continue to the next step. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
|  

&#124; Page 311 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 6\. In step 5, if you accidentally omit the -l option, you could delete all your current ongoing cron jobs. If you lose the root users cron jobs, important system functions will be disabled. The rest of this step discusses how to try to save your cron jobs if you accidentally omit the -l option. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; The missing -l option puts your current crontabs in jeopardy. You will then see the PS2 prompt (usually the greater-than sign), which means the shell is waiting for input from the keyboard to replace your current crontabs. Press your INTR key (usually Ctrl+C or DEL) to abort this command. If the INTR key fails, go to another port and run step 5 correctly. Then come back to this port and enter your EOT key (usually Ctrl+D) to wipe out your current crontabs. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; To avoid the dreaded PS2 prompt completely, some users use this command instead of that described in step 5: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; cp /usr/spool/cron/crontabs/MYID cronfile  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Replace *MYID* in this line with your login id name. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Some users use crontab -e (which automatically invokes the default EDITOR). However, if you forget the -e option, you still face the same problem described in this step. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 7\. Enter vi cronfile. (You can use any text editor to edit this file.) Now you should see all of your current ongoing cron jobs in the six-field format discussed earlier. For example, you might see the following line: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 17 5 * * 0 /etc/cleanup > /dev/null  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; If your login account has never submitted a cron job before, this cronfile will be empty. If this cronfile is empty but it is not supposed to be empty (for instance, the roots cronfile should not be empty), go back to step 1 and start over. If you have lost your prior cron entries, you will have to key them all in again. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 8\. Use the text editor to modify any existing cron jobs and add new onesin the six-field formatto this file. If you created a cron script in step 3 of this procedure, add a new six-field line to that file, with the full pathname of your cron script in the last field. When you finish editing, save your work and &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
|  

&#124; Page 312 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; exit from the editor. This cronfile is just a temporary file, so if you dont like your saved results, go back to step 5 and start over. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 9\. Enter cat cronfile. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Make sure that this file contains proper six-field entries for all previous cron jobs to be retained, plus any modified or new cron jobs youve added. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;  &#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Note &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;  &#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Remember that this file must contain all cron jobs to run for this login. If you delete an entry from this file, you will be deleting it from cron, and it wont run in the future. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 10\. Enter crontab cronfile. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; This will submit your cron changes, replacing all of your previous cron jobs. If you get an error saying that you are not allowed to submit cron jobs, see the later section Enabling and Disabling cron/at/batch by User. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 11\. Enter crontab -l to display your current crontab entries as submitted. Then review the warnings about this command that appeared earlier in this procedure. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; SEE ALSO &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; ![sarrow.gif](content/ad91af06ad96c57f0a338bded4c42f0e.gif)*For more information on editing with* vi, *see pages 449 and 471* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; ![sarrow.gif](content/ad91af06ad96c57f0a338bded4c42f0e.gif)*For more information on displaying a file, see page 147* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; *Using the Asterisk (*) Wildcard in Crontabs.* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; crontab allows an asterisk (*) wildcard to be used as shown in Table 12.4\. Note that it is a crontab wildcard, not a Filename Generation Wildcard nor a regular expression wildcard. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;  &#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Tips on crontab field 1: the minute of the hour &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;  &#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; If you find an asterisk in field 1 (to run your job 60 times in one hour), it is usually a mistake. Avoid putting a zero in the minute field for every cron job because that could hurt system performance at the start of every hour. Stagger the minute values for those jobs that dont have to start exactly on the hour. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  

&#124; Table 12.4 Using the asterisk (^*) wildcard in *crontabs.* &#124;
&#124; *crontabs* Field &#124; What an Asterisk Means in That Field &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124; 1. minute of the hour &#124; Do job every minute, 60 times per hour &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124; 2. hour of the day &#124; Do job every hour, 24 times per day &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124; 3. day of the month &#124; Ignore this field and use field 5^* &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124; 4. month of the year &#124; Do job every month, 12 months per year &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124; 5. day of the week &#124; Ignore this field and use field 3^* &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124; ^**An asterisk in both fields 3 and 5 means the job is to run every day.* &#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
|  

&#124; Page 313 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; *Running Early Morning Weekday Jobs* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Here is a typical crontab error: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 30 1 * * 1-5 /u/backup &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; This company works Monday through Friday and wants to execute a backup at 1:30 a.m. after every work day. However, with this command, Fridays work will not be backed up until Monday morning at 1:30 a.m. Because heavy building maintenance work and power problems are more frequent on weekends, this is not good. Here is the corrected entry, which will also run the backup on Saturday morning: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 30 1 * * 2-6 /u/backup &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; For the same reason, this would not be a good entry for that company: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 30 1 * * * /u/backup &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Because no one is in the office on Saturday and Sunday, the tape will not be changed, and Friday nights backup (which really runs early Saturday) will be rewritten Saturday night and Sunday night. A power problem over the weekend could corrupt files, and then those corrupted files would replace the good Friday night backup. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; SEE ALSO &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; ![sarrow.gif](content/ad91af06ad96c57f0a338bded4c42f0e.gif)*For more information on backups, see page 327* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; *Scheduling One-Time Jobs at a Specific Date/Time (*at*)* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; The UNIX at command allows you to schedule a job to run once at a later predetermined time. If you want to run the job more than once (periodically, for example), see the previous section on the crontab command. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Scheduling a Job Using the at Command &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 1\. Log in as the user whose account will be used to run the job. Use root only if it is absolutely necessary. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 2\. Enter at, but do not press the Enter key until you are instructed to do so. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
|  

&#124; Page 314 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 3\. Enter a space, and then indicate when to run the command using one of these three methods: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Method 1 is to enter a time only, for example: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 3 &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; means 3 a.m. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 17 &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; means 5 p.m. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 0704 &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; means 7:04 a.m. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 7:04pm &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; means 7:04 p.m. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;

 &#124;

&#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; The job will run within the next 24 hours at the requested time. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Method 2 is to enter a time and day, for example: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 2pm Sat &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 1923 Aug 24 &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 7:04pm tomorrow &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; The job will run within the next year at the requested time on the requested day. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Method 3 is to give an offset, for example: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; now + 5 min &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; now + 2 days &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 4\. Press the Enter key to execute this line. The cursor will go down to the next line that has no prompt character and wait there for more input. If you get an error at this point, see the later section Enabling and Disabling crontab/at/batch by User. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 5\. Enter the command that you want to run later. Enter it exactly as you would enter it to run it normally. Then press the Enter key to submit the command. You can continue to enter more commands to be executed in sequence. Press the Enter key after each one. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 6\. When you finish entering commands, the cursor should be at the start of a blank line. Enter your EOT key (usually Ctrl+D), and your normal shell prompt should appear. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
|  

&#124; Page 315 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; You can use the -l option with the at command to list your current scheduled jobs. You can use the -r option to remove scheduled jobs. The following example illustrates the use of these options. It also shows a quick command you might want to use for testing the at command. It will create a junk file in the current directory in five minutes if you dont remove the job. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; $ at now + 5 min date > junk
warning: commands will be executed using /bin/sh
job 888071220.a-9910:0 at Sat Feb 21 06:27:00 1998
$ at -l
888071220.a-9910:0      Sat Feb 21 06:27:00 1998
$ at -r 888071220.a
at: 888071220.a does not exist: No such file or directory
![arrow.gif](content/4505ed21b36efb4ebf4df5206fc03bad.gif)(error 2)
$ at -r 888071220.a-9910:0
$ at -l
$ &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; In the above example, notice that the -l option to the at command shows when the job will run, but it does not show which command will be run. Notice the -r option requires that the full job id be entered. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; If the system is down at the time and day the at job is supposed to run, the at job will be run as soon as the system is brought up again (unlike cron). You can even write an at job that will queue itself up to run again periodically. You do so by adding a line like this at the end of the at script: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; echo "sh jobname" &#124; at 2330 sat next week &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; *Scheduling One-Time Jobs to Run When the Load Is Light (*batch*)* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; The batch command can be used to run a job whenever the system feels the load is light enoughwhich means you cant predict when it will run. If your system is always heavily loaded, batch is not a useful command for you because it will never be able to start your job. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
|  

&#124; Page 316 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Using the Batch Command &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 1\. Enter batch and press the Enter key. The cursor will go down to the next line with no prompt character, where it will wait for more input. If you get an error at this point, see the later section Enabling and Disabling crontab/at/batch by User. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 2\. Enter the command that you want to run later. Enter it exactly as you would enter it to run it normally. Press the Enter key to submit the command. You can continue to enter more commands to be performed in sequence. Press the Enter key after each one. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 3\. When you finish entering commands, the cursor should be at the start of a blank line. Enter your EOT key (usually Ctrl+D), and your normal shell prompt should appear. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; *Enabling and Disabling crontab/at/batch by User* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; The root user (system administrator) can modify these two files to allow or deny users to use crontabs: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; /usr/lib/cron/cron.allow /usr/lib/cron/cron.deny &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; The root user also can modify the following two files to allow/deny users to use the at or batch commands: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; /usr/lib/cron/at.allow /usr/lib/cron/at.deny &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; If the allow files exist, only users listed in that file can use the command. The deny files are used only if the allow files do not exist. In that case, all users can use the command except those listed in the deny file. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Job Priorities. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; The following sections cover the commands necessary to view and change the priorities of running processes. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
|  

&#124; Page 317 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; *Viewing Jobs and Their Priority (*ps*)* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; You can use the -lf options with ps to show each running process (job) and its current priority. For example, take a look at this code: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; $ ps -lf &#124; pg   F S      UID   PID  PPID  C PRI NI     ADDR   SZ
![arrow.gif](content/4505ed21b36efb4ebf4df5206fc03bad.gif)WCHAN    STIME     TTY        TIME CMD
20 S     mori  9998  9374  6  73 20 fb11e798  132  fb11e798
![arrow.gif](content/4505ed21b36efb4ebf4df5206fc03bad.gif)06:54:41 ttyR030    00:00:00 -ksh
20 O     mori 10020  9998  7  48 20 fb11e8f0  160
![arrow.gif](content/4505ed21b36efb4ebf4df5206fc03bad.gif)- 06:55:23 ttyR030    00:00:00 ps -lf
30 S     mori 10021  9998  2  78 20 fb11ecf8   72  fb11ecf9
![arrow.gif](content/4505ed21b36efb4ebf4df5206fc03bad.gif)06:55:23 ttyR030    00:00:00 pg &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; The column labeled NI shows the process nice value (in this case, 20). The higher the nice value, the lower its priority to get system resources and time (the nicer it is to everyone else on the system). Table 12.5 outlines typical nice values. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  

&#124; Table 12.5 *nice* (priority) values. &#124;
&#124; Type of System &#124; Allowed range for *nice* values &#124; Default value &#124;
&#124; System V &#124; 0 to 39 &#124; 20 &#124;
&#124; BSD &#124; -20 to +20 &#124; 0 &#124;

 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; *Starting a Job with Low Priority (*nice*)* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Starting a Job with Low Priority (*nice*) &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 1\. Enter nice, but do not press the Enter key until you are instructed to do so. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 2\. Enter a space and then enter -VAL, replacing *VAL* with a number between 1 and 19\. The larger the value, the nicer you will be to other users on the system; the slower your job will run. The root user (only) can enter --VAL to lower the nice value and hence raise his job priority above other users. The root user must be careful, however, not to raise the priority so high that the job takes over and disables all other system functions. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
|  

&#124; Page 318 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 3\. Enter a space and then enter the desired command to run. If you enter a pipeline, enter a nice command for each stage of the pipeline. (See the next example.) Press the Enter key to execute your command. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;  &#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Your nice or renice may differ &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;  &#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Check your man, pages on nice and renice. On some systems, the range of nice values and whether to enter them as positive or negative may differ from whats described here. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; This example shows that the nice command must be explicitly invoked for each command in a pipeline. This command pipes the output of ps to pg. Note also that ps has a nice increment of 5, and pg has a nice increment of 7\. Different values were chosen just to illustrate a point; normally you would use the same value for both. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; $ nice -5 ps -lf &#124; nice -7 pg   F S      UID   PID  PPID  C PRI NI     ADDR   SZ
![arrow.gif](content/4505ed21b36efb4ebf4df5206fc03bad.gif)WCHAN    STIME     TTY        TIME CMD
20 S     mori 10042  9996  5  73 20 fb11e798  132  fb11e798
![arrow.gif](content/4505ed21b36efb4ebf4df5206fc03bad.gif)07:12:35 ttyR029    00:00:00 -ksh
20 O     mori 10066 10042  9  44 25 fb11e8f0  160
![arrow.gif](content/4505ed21b36efb4ebf4df5206fc03bad.gif)- 07:13:24 ttyR029    00:00:00 ps -lf
20 S     mori 10067 10042  5  76 27 fb11ecf8   72  f093d7c0
![arrow.gif](content/4505ed21b36efb4ebf4df5206fc03bad.gif)07:13:24 ttyR029    00:00:00 pg
$ &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Notice the pg command has a nice value of 27\. Thats because nice -7 means to raise the nice value 7 points from the default of 20. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; *Changing the Priority of an Existing Job (*renice*)* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Modern UNIX systems support a renice command to allow you to change the nice value of a process that has already been started. However, you must first look up the PID value for the desired process using the ps command (see the previous ps example). &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;  &#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Note &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;  &#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; See the glossary for the definition of PID value. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Changing the Priority of an Existing Job (*renice*) &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 1\. Enter the renice command, but do not press the Enter key until you are instructed to do so. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 2\. Enter a space and then the -n option. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 3\. Enter a space and then VAL, where *VAL* is a number between 1 and 19\. This represents the amount to raise the nice value and hence lower the priority of the job. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
|  

&#124; Page 319 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 4\. Enter a space followed by the PID number for the process (job) you want to change. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 5\. Your command should look something like this: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; renice -n 5 10042 &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Press the Enter key to execute your command. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;  &#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  &#124; When to use nice, at, and batch &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;  &#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Use nice or renice when you need the job to complete quickly but you want to minimize the impact on other users. Use at to make sure the job does not run until the time specified. Use batch to make productive use of system idle time, but dont use batch on a system that is constantly busy. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Background Jobs &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; UNIX is a multi-tasking operating system. This means that, in general, you can start more than one job, and all will run concurrently. Your station is not tied up waiting for them to finish. You can even specify sequences of jobs so that one job will not start until the previous job has completed. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; *Starting Background Jobs (&).* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; To start a job in the background, simply end the UNIX command with a space and then an ampersand (&), as shown in this example: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; $ make acmesys > acme.log 2>&1 & 27903
$ &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Heres a breakdown of the parts of that command: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; make is a command that can take a long time to complete; therefore, you might run it in the background so it does not tie up your station. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; > acme.log redirects the output from make into a file called acme.log. This is often a good idea when youre starting background because the output is saved for later review. If you dont redirect the output in this way, it will still go to your screen where it could mix with other output. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 2>&1 redirects any error messages from the make command so they will go to the same file as the standard output (so youre saving output and errors from make in the same file). &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 27903 is the job number, which is also called a process id number or PID. If you save this number, you can use it later to check on this job. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
|  

&#124; Page 320 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; *Preventing Logoff from Killing Background Jobs (*nohup*)* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Logging off the system usually terminates all background jobs. Some shells will warn you that you have stopped jobs. If you then type exit a second time, you will terminate those jobs and log off. The nohup command allows you to start background jobs that will not be killed when you log off. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Starting Background Jobs Using nohup &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 1\. At the shell prompt, enter nohup. Do not press the Enter key until you are instructed to do so. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 2\. Enter a space and then the UNIX command you want to run. Remember to redirect standard output and standard error messages if desired. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 3\. Enter a space and then the ampersand (&). &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 4\. Press the Enter key to execute your command in the background. Now your logoff will not terminate that background job. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; If you do not redirect standard output and standard errors, the nohup command will automatically create a file called nohup.out to save them in. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; *Killing a Background Job (*kill*)* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; If you write down the PID that is displayed when you start a background job, it is easy to terminate that job using either of two kill commands. The following procedures shows you how to use both commands. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; How to Terminate a Job by Its PID &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 1\. From the shell prompt, enter kill PID, where *PID* is the PID number of the process you want to terminate. Double-check that you have entered the number correctly. Then press the Enter key. This kill command gives the job a &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
|  

&#124; Page 321 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; chance to terminate gracefully, closing applications and removing lock files and temporary files. No messages will be displayed. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 2\. Now enter the command kill -9 PID, where *PID* is the same number you used in step 1\. Double-check that you have entered the number correctly. Then press Enter. This kill will end even uncooperative commands. Although you can execute step 2 immediately after step 1, you might want to wait two seconds to let step 1 wrap up. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 3\. If step 2 gives the error No such PID, ignore that error. It just means that step 1 was enough to end the task, and step 2 was unnecessary but not harmful. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; If you dont remember your PID number, you can look it up using the ps command. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Using ps to find a PID Number &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 1\. From the shell prompt, enter these two commands: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; ps -ef ps aux &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Some systems support both of these commands, but sometimes only one gives results. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 2\. Using the command that works on your system, look at the initial heading to find the PID column, the user (UID) column, and the command (CMD) column. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 3\. If necessary, rerun the command and pipe it to pg, more, or less to see it a page at a time. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Alternatively, you can pipe the output of the ps command to grep to filter out the lines you dont care about. Note that this will also remove the heading. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 4\. Locate the command that you want to terminate. Check the user column to make sure you started this command. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 5\. Locate the PID for that command. Then you can follow the procedure for terminating a job by its PID. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Here is an example of a command used to find a background job. However, the output was cut off in mid-process. Because ps can show so many processes, the command was aborted using ^C (on Solaris). &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
|  

&#124; Page 322 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; # ps -ef      UID   PID  PPID  C    STIME TTY      TIME CMD
    root     0     0  0   Feb 20 ?        0:02 sched
    root     1     0  0   Feb 20 ?        0:15 /etc/init -
    root     2     0  0   Feb 20 ?        0:00 pageout
    root     3     0  0   Feb 20 ?        1:02 fsflush
    root   289     1  0   Feb 20 ?        0:00
    ![arrow.gif](content/4505ed21b36efb4ebf4df5206fc03bad.gif)/usr/lib/saf/sac -t 300 &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Suppose you were running the previous command to look for a find command that was started earlier. You could use grep to filter out the lines you dont want, as shown here: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; # ps -ef&#124;grep find     root 27961 27955  5 13:53:33 pts/1    0:03 find / -name
    ![arrow.gif](content/4505ed21b36efb4ebf4df5206fc03bad.gif)acme -print
    root 27967 27955  0 13:54:19 pts/1    0:00 grep find
# &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; From the CMD field (the last field), you can see that two processes mentioning find were found. Looking at field 2, you see that PID 27961 is the find process you want to terminate. Notice that PID 27967 is the grep process that was looking for find; in other words, grep saw itself while it was looking for find. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Here is a similar example that uses an additional grep -v to remove the extraneous grep process from the output: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; # ps -ef &#124; grep find &#124; grep -v grep     root 27961 27955  5 13:53:33 pts/1    0:03 find / -name
    ![arrow.gif](content/4505ed21b36efb4ebf4df5206fc03bad.gif)acme -print
# &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; When you know the PID you want to terminate, you can canenter these lines to kill the process: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; kill 27961 kill -9 27961 &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; SEE ALSO &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; ![sarrow.gif](content/ad91af06ad96c57f0a338bded4c42f0e.gif)*For more information on* grep, *see page 380* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Extra Job Control Under the Korn Shell &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; In the previous section, we covered use of background jobs that would apply to all shells, including the Bourne shell. Newer &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
|  

&#124; Page 323 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; shells have made it much easier to work with background jobs by adding a feature called *job control*. For example, some systems have added job control to the Bourne shell, which can be invoked as jsh. This section describes the other job control commands, which are similar to jsh: They are csh for the C shell and ksh for the Korn shell. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; *Listing Background Jobs (*jobs*).* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; To list all background jobs in any shell supporting job control, go to the shell prompt and enter jobs. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; You will see output like this: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; $ jobs [4] +  Running              find / -name acme -print >
![arrow.gif](content/4505ed21b36efb4ebf4df5206fc03bad.gif)/tmp/acme.find &
[3] - Stopped (SIGTSTP)     man find
[2]   Stopped (SIGTSTP)     bc
[1]   Stopped (SIGTSTP)     vi acmereport
$ &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; The job number is given in brackets at the start of each line. The job most recently in the foreground (that was most recently active on your screen) is indicated by a plus sign (+). The second most recent job is indicated by a minus sign (-). Notice that you no longer have to worry about PID numbers. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; *Suspending and Resuming Jobs (Ctrl+Z,* bg, fg*)* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; One of the most powerful applications of job control is to take a foreground job (one that is tying up your keyboard and screen), suspend it in the background so you can enter other commands, and then retrieve the suspended job later. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; In some SCO UNIX operating systems, very few utilities honor the Ctrl+Z method for doing this; in those systems vi is the only command that works. Under Solaris and AIX, however, Ctrl+Z seems to work for every utility. You can use it to move jobs very easily between the foreground and the background. This was true in the Korn shell but not under jsh. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
|  

&#124; Page 324 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Moving a Job to the Background and Back to the Foreground &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 1\. Make sure you are in a shell that supports job control, such as the Korn shell (not the Bourne shell). If you are not sure, invoke the Korn shell with the command exec ksh. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Enter any UNIX command that will take some time to complete. Do not enter a final ampersand (&) to the command, and the job will run in the foreground and tie up your keyboard and screen. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 2\. To move that job to the background, press Ctrl+Z. You should see an acknowledgment like this, specifying the command you were running: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; ^Z[1] + Stopped (SIGTSTP)        find / -name acme ![arrow.gif](content/4505ed21b36efb4ebf4df5206fc03bad.gif) -print &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; If you do not see such a message, either your shell does not support job control or your version of UNIX does not support the use of Ctrl+Z to suspend all jobs. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; You will now have a system prompt, at which you can enter other commands. Your previous job is suspended (its no longer running). &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 3\. Enter jobs, and you will see output like this: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; [2] + Stopped (SIGTSTP)     find / -name acme -print > ![arrow.gif](content/4505ed21b36efb4ebf4df5206fc03bad.gif)/tmp/acme.find &
[1] - Stopped (SIGTSTP)     man find &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 4\. To allow the job to continue running in the background, at the shell prompt, enter bg %JOBID, where *JOBID* is the job number shown by the jobs command. If the job is the most recent jobas denoted by the plus sign (+)you can omit %JOBID altogether. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 5\. Enter jobs again. Now you should see output like this, indicating that your job is running: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; [2] +  Running              find / -name acme -print > ![arrow.gif](content/4505ed21b36efb4ebf4df5206fc03bad.gif)/tmp/acme.find &
[1] - Stopped (SIGTSTP)     man find &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 6\. To bring your job back to the foreground, at the shell prompt, enter fg %JOBID, where *JOBID* is the number of the job you want to bring to the foreground. The command &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
|  

&#124; Page 325 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; being run will appear on the screen, and the specified job will again have control of your keyboard and screen. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; *Killing a Background Job Under the Korn Shell* (kill) &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; With job control, it is easy to terminate a background job. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Terminating a Background Job using Job Control &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 1\. At the shell prompt, enter jobs to determine the job number of the job you want to terminate. This should be small number, no greater than the total number of jobs displayed. This is *not* a PID number. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 2\. Enter the command kill %JOBID, where *JOBID* is the number of the job to be terminated. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Or, to terminate the most recent job, you can enter kill%%. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Or, to terminate the second most recent job, you can enter kill%-. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; *Pausing Background Jobs Just Before They Output* (stty) &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Some background jobs will compute for a long time and then display a result. You may want the compute phase to continue in the background but then have the job suspend itself until you are ready for the output. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Suspending Jobs just before They Output &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 1\. At the shell prompt, enter stty tostop. This will cause any new background jobs to suspend just before they start any output. This mode will last until you log off. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 2\. Enter your desired UNIX command, ending in an ampersand (&) so it runs in the background. Press Enter. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 3\. At the shell prompt, enter jobs. From the output of the jobs command, determine whether the background job is running. If the state of the background job is running, it is not yet ready to display any output. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 4\. When the jobs command shows that your desired background job is stopped, it is ready to provide some output. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
|  

&#124; Page 326 &#124;

&#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;  &#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Note &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;  &#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; You can put the command stty tostop in your .profile file if you want it set automatically every time you log in. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Enter fg %JOBID, where *JOBID* is the number of the stopped job. This will bring the job to the foreground and start the output so that you can see the output on your screen at a time of your choosing. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 |

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
