&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; grep, egrep, fgrep sed
awk
perl &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
|  

&#124; Page 395 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; vi (when searching and substituting) &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; ed (when searching and substituting) &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; *Comparing Filename Wildcards with Regular Expression Wildcards* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Sometimes people are confused about when to use regular expressions and when to use Filename Generation Wildcard patterns. The following guidelines should alleviate some of the confusion: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Use regular expressions when you want to search the contents of files or pipelines for patterns. Only a handful of commands support the use of regular expressions; see the previous section. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Use Filename Generation Wildcard patterns when you want to create a list of filenames based on a pattern. Many UNIX commands will accept a list of files on the command line. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; *Allowing Any Characters in Certain Pattern Positions (*.*)* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; The period (.) is a regular expression wildcard. It represents any single character, which enables you to specify exactly how many character positions to allow before, after, or between other pattern elements. The following command shows an example of the period character in use: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; grep 'dog.bone' report7 &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Given this command, grep would display all lines that contain dog, followed by any single character, followed by bone. For example, it might return lines that contain the following strings: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; dog-bone dog bone
dog/bone
dogEbone &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
|  

&#124; Page 396 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; It would not, however, display a line containing dogbone because there is no character separating dog and bone in that case. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; To specify that you want to match an actual period (.) in a regular expression, you precede the period with a backslash (\) like this: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; grep '5\.25' report7 &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; This command would display any lines containing 5.25\. The backslash (\) is needed before the period to prevent grep from thinking the period is a regular expression wildcard that matches any character. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; *Specifying Allowed Characters in Pattern Positions (*[...]*)* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Square brackets allow you to specify a set of alternatives for the character in that position within a regular expression, as shown in the following example: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; grep 'dog[- EZ1-3]bone' report7 &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Given this command, grep would display lines that contain any of the following strings: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; dog-bone dog bone
dogEbone
dogZbone
dog1bone
dog2bone
dog3bone &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Note, however, that unless other allowed dog bone references were included in the lines, grep would not display lines that contain the following strings: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; dog4bone (because 4 is not an allowed alternative) &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; dogEZbone (because the square brackets represent only a single character within the pattern) &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
|  

&#124; Page 397 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; dogbone (because there is no single character between dog and bone) &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Inside the brackets [], a dash (-) between two letters or digits indicates an inclusive range. To indicate a literal dash (-) as a character in the list, you must place it first or last in the list. To indicate a right bracket (]) as a character in the list, place it as the first list element as in []abc]. A period (.), asterisk (*), left bracket ([), or backslash (\) inside the brackets is treated as a literal character without special meaning. Consider, then, the following command: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; grep '[0-9][0-9][0-9]' report7 &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Here, grep displays any lines containing three (or more) consecutive digits. Even if you are only searching for three digits, grep might find more than three digits because the pattern does not prohibit more digits before or after the three digits. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Here is another example: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; grep '^[A-Z]' report7 &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Given this command, grep will display all lines that begin with a capital letter. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; *Specifying Disallowed Characters in Pattern Positions (*[^...]*)* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; If the list in square brackets begins with a circumflex (^), it will match any single character except for the ones in the list. For example, given the following command &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; grep 'acme[^0-9]' report7 &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; grep will display all lines containing acme followed by one character, as long as that character is not a digit. It will not display lines that end with acme because there must be one character following acme in this pattern. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Here is another example: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; grep '^[^a-zA-Z]' report7 &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
|  

&#124; Page 398 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; This command will display all lines that start with some character other than a letter. It will not display empty lines, however, because some non-letter character must be present. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;  &#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Have we seen this before? &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;  &#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; The square brackets in Filename Generation Wildcards are very similar to regular expression wildcards. However, to disallow the characters in brackets, Filename Generation Wildcards put an exclamation point (!) as the first character while regular expression wildcards put a circumflex (^) as the first character. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; *Specifying Number of Occurrences of a Regular Expression Element (*{}*)* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; When specifying regular expressions, you can use a shorthand method of specifying the number of occurrences of the previous regular expression element. This shorthand method uses escaped braces: \{ and \}. Heres an example of a command with escaped braces: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; grep '2[0-9]\{10\}000' report7 &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; In this command, the regular expression tells grep to look for a 2, followed by exactly 10 digits, followed by 000. grep does *not* read this as a 2, followed by any digit, followed by 10 more digits. It reads this as a 2, followed by 10 occurrences of a digit (not 11 occurrences), followed by 000. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Specifying Number of Occurrences of an Element &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 1\. At the shell prompt, enter your desired command containing a regular expression. Enter the pattern element that is to be repeated. This pattern element can be a simple letter, a digit, or a regular expression wildcard such as a period (.) or brackets []. Do not press the Enter key until youre instructed to do so. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 2\. Enter \{. (Do not enter any spaces unless youre instructed to do so.) &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 3\. Enter the desired number of occurrences of the previous pattern element. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 4\. If that number is a minimum number and you want to allow the pattern to be repeated more times than that, enter a comma (,). &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 5\. If there is a maximum number of times you want to allow the pattern element to be repeated, enter that number now. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 6\. Enter \}. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
|  

&#124; Page 399 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 7\. Now complete the rest of your regular expression and the command. When you finish, press Enter to execute your command. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Consider the following example: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; grep '$[0-9]\{3,5\}\.' report7 &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Given this command, grep would display all lines that contain a dollar sign ($), followed by at least three digits but not more than five digits, followed by a period (.) Note that because the period is escaped, it is not a wildcard. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Heres another example: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; grep '[a-zA-Z]\{20,\}' report7 &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; This command would display all lines that contain words of 20 or more upper- or lowercase letters. Note that the comma is superfluous here; youll learn why in the section on unbounded or more wildcards. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; *Specifying Zero or More Occurrences of a Regular Expression Element (***).* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; The asterisk is a regular expression wildcard that you can use as a shorthand method for this expression: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; \{0,\} &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; The asterisk (*) tells grep to allow zero or more occurrences of the previous regular expression element. Dont confuse this with the asterisk (*) Filename Generation Wildcard, which means something different and is used in a totally different context. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; The following command shows you how to use the asteriskregular expression wildcard: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; grep 'ab*c' report7 &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; In this command, b* indicates that grep should allow zero or more bs. Given this command, grep would display lines that contain any of the following strings: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; ac (0 occurrences of b) &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
|  

&#124; Page 400 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; abc (1 occurrence of b) &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; abbc (2 occurrences of b) &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; abbbc (3 occurrences of b) &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; abbbbc (4 occurrences of b) &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; and so on, including &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; abbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbc &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;  &#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Why do UNIX scripts contain [ ] &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;  &#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Because there are spaces or tabs at the left margin, some grep commands can contain a pattern like ^[]*acme.. The characters within the square brackets are one space and one tab. This pattern looks for acme immediately after the left margin of zero or more spaces or tabs. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; To indicate zero or more occurrences of any character, you can use the period and the asterisk together (.*), as in this example: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; grep 'dog.*bone' report7 &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; This command would display lines that contain the following strings: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; dogbone dog-bone
doggy bone
My dog has a bone.
My dog is named Rover. Please add a soup bone to the grocery list. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; The above command would not display cases where dog is on one line and bone is on the next. The whole regular expression must be on one line. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; As another example, this command &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; grep '[0-9]*' report7 &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; would display all lines that contain zero or more digits. Every line of the file would be displayed because every line of the file will contain zero or more digits. (Count the digits in each line and you will see that I am right.) &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; grep '[0-9][0-9]*' report7 &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; This command displays any line containing one digit followed by zero or more digits. Essentially, this finds and displays all lines with one or more digits. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; grep '$[0-9][0-9]*\.' report7 &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
|  

&#124; Page 401 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Given this command, grep displays any lines that contain a dollar sign ($), followed by one or more digits, followed by a period (.). The previous command is also equivalent to this one: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; grep '$[0-9]\{1,\}\.' report7 &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Anytime you see two consecutive occurrences of a regular expression element followed by an asterisk (*), remember that you can find one or more of that element by using a command such as this: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; grep 'abb*c' report7 &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; This command tells grep to display any lines that contain a, followed by one or more bs, followed by a c. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; *Dropping Unbounded ''or more'' Regular Expression Wildcards* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; UNIX offers several ways for you to indicate that an element is to be used a certain number of times or more. For example, you could use any of the following expressions: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; a\{6,\}        (6 or more of the letter a) b*             (0 or more of the letter b)
cc*            (1 or more of the letter c)
ddd*           (2 or more of the letter d) &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Compare these two commands: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; grep '[0-9]\{3,\}' report7 grep '[0-9]\{3\}' report7 &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; The first of these commands will display lines that contain three or more digits. The second command will display lines that contain three digits. However the second command does not specify limitations on what characters may come after those three digits. Thus the second command will allow more digits after the three digits. In other words, it will also display lines containing three or more digits. In other words, the two commands will both display the exact same output even though you specified or more in the first command but not in the second. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; The same is true for these two commands: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; grep 'abb*' report7 grep 'ab' report7 &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
|  

&#124; Page 402 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; The first command will display lines containing a, followed by one or more bs. The second command will display lines containing ab. The two commands are equivalent, however, because any line that contains a, followed by one or more bs also contains a, followed by one b (and vice versa). The command without the or more is better, though, because it is more efficient and easier to understand, and you can predict the results. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; I call these unbounded or more situations because you are not specifying pattern elements before and after the or more element. If the or more element is unbounded, either before or after the element, omit the or more part from your grep command. This will make the grep command more efficient, and you will better understand what lines your grep command will output. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Here are some bounded or more situations: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; grep "abb*c" report7 grep '^[0-9]*$' report7
grep '$[0-9]\{5,\}\.' report7 &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; In each of these commands, pattern elements have been specified both before and after the or more wildcards. Here the or more is significant, however; if you leave it out, you will change the output from the command. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Extra Regular Expression Wildcards Available in egrep &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; The egrep command is an extended version of grep that allows some regular expression wildcards grep doesnt allow. However, egrep does not support the braces {} wildcard to specify the number of occurrences. Sometimes the set of egrep regular expression wildcards are called *extended regular expressions* or *full regular expressions*. The syntax for egrep is the same as that for grep. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
|  

&#124; Page 403 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; *Specifying One Or More Occurrences of an Element with egrep (*+*)* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; To specify that the previous pattern element is to be used one or more times, you use the plus sign (+) wildcard with egrep, as shown here: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; egrep 'ab+c' report7 &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; This command would display lines that contain a, followed by one or more bs, followed by c. The plus sign (+) wildcard is not supported by grep. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; *Using a Regular Expression Element Zero or More Times with egrep (*?*)* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; To specify zero or one occurrence of an element, you can use the question mark (?) with egrep: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; egrep 'Mrs?. Smith' report7 &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; The above command would display lines that contain strings such as these: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Mr. Smith Mrs. Smith &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; However, it would not display lines with Mrss. Smith. The question mark (?) must be preceded by a backslash (\) or enclosed in double or single quotation marks (as shown). The question mark (?) wildcard is not supported by grep. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; *Searching for One of Several Patterns (&#124;)* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Using egrep, you can search for and display lines that contain one of several patterns. You separate those patterns with the vertical bar (&#124;), which is also used as the pipe sign (&#124;). Heres an example: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; egrep 'acme&#124;pegasus&#124;apollo' report7 &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
|  

&#124; Page 404 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; This command will display lines that contain acme or pegasus or apollo. The vertical bar (&#124;) must be preceded by a backslash (\) or enclosed in double or single quotation marks (as shown). &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Parentheses () can be used to group the vertical bar (&#124;) choices, as shown here: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; egrep 'project (acme&#124;pegasus&#124;apollo)' report7 &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; This command will display lines that contain project acme or project pegasus or apollo. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Extra Regular Expression Wildcards Available Only in perl &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; perl is a complete programming language that runs under UNIX and Windows. While it usually does not come with any commercial UNIX distribution, it is readily available via the Internet for most UNIX systems. If perl is available on your system, you can use it as a grep-like command-line utility that provides search and display capabilities not available in grep or egrep. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Using Perl to Find Lines with Patterns. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 1\. If you are going to use perl in a pipeline, enter the UNIX command sequence that will generate the output for perl to process. End this sequence with a pipe sign (&#124;). Do not press Enter until youre instructed to do so. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 2\. Enter perl -ne 'print if /. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; The -e option to perl allows you to enter a line of perl code on the command line. The -n option allows perl to process each line of standard input or any files specified on the command line. Do not press Enter until youre instructed todo so. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 3\. Enter the pattern to search for. You can include any of the regular expressions for grep and also those for egrep. Braces {} to indicate a repeat count should not be preceded by a backslash (\) as they are with grep. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
|  

&#124; Page 405 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 4\. Enter /. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 5\. If you want to ignore case in the pattern, enter i. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 6\. If you want to ignore spaces in the pattern, enter x. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 7\. Enter a single quotation mark (). &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 8\. If you are not piping to perl, enter a space and then enter one or more filenames to search. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 9\. Press the Enter key to execute your command. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Here is a complete example: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; perl -ne 'print if /^acme [0-9] {3,} \ /ix' report7 report8 &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; This command illustrates that complex regular expressions are easier to read using perl. The regular expression is found between the slashes (/) in the command. If you use the perl x option after the closing slash (/), spaces are ignored in the regular expression unless they are escapedpreceded by a backslash (\). Think of the x as allowing you to expand the pattern, using spaces freely to make it more readable. The other perl feature that improves readability is that backslashes (\) are not used before braces {} indicating repeat counts. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; *Finding Words That Are Not Parts of Larger Words (*\b*)* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Using perl, you can search for words that are not part of larger words. This is difficult or impossible using grep or egrep. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; To specify a word boundary, enter \b in the regular expression for perl. With perl, a word can contain upper- or lowercase letters, digits, or the underscore character (_). &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; perl -ne 'print if /\b in \b/ix' report7 &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; In this example, the regular expression is placed within slashes (/). Again, you use the x option following the final slash (/) so that spaces can be inserted in the regular expression to improve readability. This command will display any lines in report7 that contain the word in. By placing \b before and after the word in, you can specify that the word in cannot be part of a larger word. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
|  

&#124; Page 406 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Therefore, the output will not display lines that contain the words tin, bin, dinner, or into, for example. However, it will display the word in if it is at the start of a line, at the end of a line, or has punctuation around it. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; In this command &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; perl -ne 'print if /\b in /ix' report7 &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; the \b occurs only before the word in. The command will display all lines that contain words that start with in, including larger words such as into or intend. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; To specify that a position not be on a word boundary, you use \B, as in this example: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; perl -ne 'print if / in \B /ix' report7 &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; This command will display all lines that contain the string in as part of a longer word such as inn or into or dinner. However the words tin and bin would not match the pattern because they have a word boundary after the word in. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; SEE ALSO &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; ![sarrow.gif](content/ad91af06ad96c57f0a338bded4c42f0e.gif)*For more information on* perl, *see page 717* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Turning Off Regular Expression Wildcards (*\,fgrep*) &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; To turn off the special nature of a regular expression wildcard, precede it with a backslash (\) as in this example: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; grep '2\*3' mathreport &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Here, you are looking for the string 2*3, so you have to turn off the special meaning of the asterisk (*). &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; If you have a large number of wildcards to turn off, you can use the fgrep command, which does not allow any regular expression wildcards. All characters are regular characters to fgrep. Therefore, with this command &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; fgrep '*****' report7 &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
|  

&#124; Page 407 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; you can look for all lines with five or more asterisks (*). You dont have to precede each one with a backslash, though, because you used the fgrep command instead of grep. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; fgrep is also useful for ignoring wildcards in the contents of shell variables, as in this example: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; fgrep "$USERINPUT" report7 &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;  &#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Two reasons to avoid fgrep &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;  &#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; fgrep is supposed to be the fast grep because ti does not have to handle regular expresions. However it is often the slowest of the grep commands. The X/Open (Ver 2) spec calls fgrep obsolete and prefers the equivalent command grep -F. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Checking Only Specific Fields to Selecta Line (*awk*) &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; awk is an extensive programming language that is available on all commercial UNIX systems. You can use a subset of it as a grep-like command-line utility that provides search and display capabilities not available in grep or egrep. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; SEE ALSO &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; ![sarrow.gif](content/ad91af06ad96c57f0a338bded4c42f0e.gif)*For more information on* awk, *see page 671* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; *Displaying a Line If Exact Match in One Field (*awk*)* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; grep checks the whole line for a match. If you want to check only a specific field of the line, you can do that using awk. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Displaying a Line Based on Exact Match in One Field &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 1\. If you are going to use awk in a pipeline, enter the UNIX command sequence that will generate the output for awk to process. End this sequence with a pipe sign (&#124;). Do not press the Enter key until youre instructed to do so. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 2\. Enter awk '$FNUM ==. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Replace *FNUM* with the field number you want to check. For awk, you separate the fields with one or more spaces or tabs. The first field is 1\. The last field can be indicated by replacing *FNUM* with NF (as in awk '$NF ==). Do not press the Enter key until youre instructed to do so. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 3\. Enter a space, and then enter the pattern to search for surrounded by double quotation marks. No wildcards are allowed. (See the next section if you want to use wildcards.) &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
|  

&#124; Page 408 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 4\. Enter a single quote (). &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 5\. If you are not piping to awk, enter a space and then enter one or more filenames to search. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 6\. Press Enter to execute your command. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Here is an example: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; awk '$3 == "acme"' report7 &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; This command will display lines of report7 in which field 3 of the line contains only the word acme. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; *Displaying a Line Based on Numeric Value in One Field (*awk*)* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; You can use the same format to display a line if a particular field contains a numeric value. No quotation marks are required around the numeric value. You can make the following tests: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;    ==   equal to    !=   not equal to
   >    greater than
   >=   greater than or equal to
   <    less than
   <=   less than or equal to
awk '$1 > 3.6' yearend.rpt &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; The previous command will display all lines in yearend.rpt in which the first field of the line contains a number larger than 3.6\. If the field starts with a letter (i.e., it is not numeric), awk treats it as an impossibly large numeric value. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; *Displaying a Line If There Is a Regular Expression Match in One Field (*awk*).* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; To use regular expressions when checking for a matching string, change the test from == to tilde (~) and put slashes (/) around the regular expressions, as shown here: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; awk '$3 ~ /^acme[0-9]/' report7 &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; This command will display all lines from report7 in which field 3 starts with acme, followed by a digit. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
|  

&#124; Page 409 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; awk allows the same regular expression wildcards as egrep, which include the following: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; + &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; for one or more occurrences of previous element &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; ? &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; for zero or one occurrences of previous element &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; &#124; &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; for allowed alternative patterns &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; () &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; for grouping patterns &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;

 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; awk, like egrep, does not allow the use of \{ \} to specify the number of occurrences. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; *Displaying a Line Based on Multiple Conditions (*&&,&#124;*&#124;)* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; To check for two conditions before displaying a line, use && to indicate a logical AND. For example, in this command: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; ls -l &#124; awk '$3 == "fred" && $5 > 2300' &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; awk is checking field 3 from ls l, which is the owner of each file. It is also checking field 5, which is the size of the file in bytes. This command will display only files owned by fred which are larger than 2300 bytes. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; To check for one condition or another being true, use &#124;&#124; to indicate a logical OR, as in this example: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; ls -l &#124; awk '$3 == "fred" &#124;&#124; $5 > 2300' &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; This command will display all files that are either owned by fred or are greater than 2300 bytes. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; To group conditions, use parentheses () like this: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; ls -l &#124; awk '( $3 == "fred" &#124;&#124; $3 == "jane") && $5 > 2300' &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; This command will display files owned by either fred or jane providing the size is greater than 2300 bytes. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
|  

&#124; Page 411 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Chapter 16 Replacing or Removing Text from a File or Pipeline &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; By Steve Mor Moritsugu &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Replacing One String with Another &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Looking for Replacements Using Regular Expression Patterns &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Using Found Text in the Replacement &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Deleting Strings &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Using Shell Variables for Replacement &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Special Replacement Capabilities in Perl &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Replacing Words That are Not Part of Larger Words (*perl*) &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
|  

&#124; Page 412 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Replacing or Removing Strings (Using Regular Expression) &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; The preceding chapter showed how to use regular expression wildcards to find lines containing a pattern within a file or pipeline. That chapter also showed that regular expression wildcards can look similar to Filename Generation Wildcards, but these are two different sets of wildcards used for totally different purposes even though they use some of the same wildcard characters. This section teaches you how to replace a substring within a line and how to use regular expression patterns to define the string to be replaced. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; SEE ALSO &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; ![sarrow.gif](content/ad91af06ad96c57f0a338bded4c42f0e.gif)*For more information on regular expression wildcards see page 388* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; *Replacing One String with Another (*sed*, regular expression)* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; To replace one string with another when displaying the output of a file, use the sed command like this: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; sed 's/Mr. Smith/Ms. Wilson/g' report7 &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; sed &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; is the stream editor. It makes any editing changes we specify as it processes the data stream one line at a time. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 's/Mr. Smith/Ms. Wilson/g' &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; is the editing command we are giving to sed. This command is usually enclosed in single quotation marks to protect the punctuation inside from shell interpretation. Use double quotation marks rather than single quotation marks if you want to include any shell variables as part of the editing command. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;

 &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
|  

&#124; Page 413 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 's/Pattern/Repl/g' &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; is the general format of the sed substitute command. Pattern is the string for which to search and Repl is the string with which to replace it. Pattern may contain regular expression wildcards, but Repl may not. Our example searches for the string Mr. Smith and replaces all occurrences of it with the string Ms. Wilson. This is true even if the Pattern is part of a larger wordfor example, Mr. Smithson would become Ms. Wilsonson. We will see later in this chapter how Perl can prevent this problem. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; report7 &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; is the file for sed to process. You can also specify a list of files, and sed will display the contents of each of them, making the substitution indicated. Filename Generation Wildcards can be used to generate the list of files. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;

 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Note that sed displays the changed output to standard output; it does not modify the file itself. The output from this command can then be piped to another command or it can be redirected to a file. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Here is the same sed command used in a pipeline situation: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; cat report* &#124; sed 's/Mr. Smith/Ms. Wilson/g' &#124; pg &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; report* is not a regular expression wildcard. It is a Filename Generation Wildcard that generates a list of all files that start with the word *report*. The cat command will output these files &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
|  

&#124; Page 414 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; on the standard output that is piped to the same sed command that we just analyzed. The output from sed will then be displayed one page at a time onscreen. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; *Using Regular Expression Wildcards in the sed Search String* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; The preceding chapter discussed regular expression (R.E.) wildcards. See the appendix under wildcard for a quick reference of all the special symbols. Here is an example sed command that uses R.E. wildcards in the search string. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; sed 's/JPC[^A-Za-z]*SPR/JPC-SPR/g' report7 &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; In this example, &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; [^A-Za-z]  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; is a regular expression wildcard that indicates any one character that is not an uppercase or lowercase letter. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; [^A-Za-z]*  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; is an regular expression wildcard that indicates zero or more occurrences of any non-letter character. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; JPC[^A-Za-z]*SPR  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; is the pattern to search for in the preceding sed command. It is looking for JPC followed by SPR with zero or more of any non-letter characters in between. That pattern can be found in each of the following lines except for the last line: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; The JPCSPR company long history of JPC-SPR relations
many JPC/SPR employees
JPC*SPR company president
four JPC(-)SPR votes
negotiate JPC SPR contracts
two companies, JPC and SPR, merged &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; In these lines, the writer has not been consistent in referring to the company name, but we can use an R.E. wildcard pattern to match all the different references and replace them with one consistent reference. The following shows how the preceding lines would be displayed after running our example sed command, which is repeated here: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
|  

&#124; Page 415 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; sed 's/JPC[^A-Za-z]*SPR/JPC-SPR/g' report7 The JPC-SPR company
long history of JPC-SPR relations
many JPC-SPR employees
JPC-SPR company president
four JPC-SPR votes
negotiate JPC-SPR contracts
two companies, JPC and SPR, merged &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Notice the last line did not match the R.E. pattern, and so no replacement was made in that line. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; *Saving the Replaced Output in the Original File (*sed*)* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; sed displays the replaced lines to standard output. If you want to replace the contents of a file, you must use two UNIX commands and a temporary file. For example: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; sed 's/pattern/repl/g' report7 > /tmp/sed$$ mv /tmp/sed$$ ![arrow.gif](content/4505ed21b36efb4ebf4df5206fc03bad.gif)report7 &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; This technique was explained in Chapter 4. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; SEE ALSO &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; ![sarrow.gif](content/ad91af06ad96c57f0a338bded4c42f0e.gif)*For more information on saving output in the original file, see page 114* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; *Making the Replacement Only Once per Line (*sed*).* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Remove the g flag from the substitute command to make the replacement a maximum of once per line. Without the g flag, we will still make the replacement once on every line where the pattern occurs, but never more than once on any given line. For example: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; sed 's/IBW/MCC/' partslist &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Assume that the file partslist, mentioned in the preceding command, contains lines like this: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 402     IBW-10    IBW(4),IBW(5) 403-6   IBW-11-6  IBW(3),MNT(16)
527     GRV-6     GRV(13,MNT(14) &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; The preceding sed command would replace those lines as follows: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
|  

&#124; Page 416 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 402     MCC-10    IBW(4),IBW(5) 403-6   MCC-11-6  IBW(3),MNT(16)
527     GRV-6     GRV(13,MNT(14) &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Notice that only the first occurrence of IBW on each line has been replaced. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; You should omit the g flag whenever you use the circumflex (^) R.E. wildcard or the dollar sign ($) R.E. wildcard (see appendix under wildcard). For example: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; sed 's/^[    ]*Chapter/Section/' book3 &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; In this example, &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; [    ] &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; is an R.E. wildcard that indicates either a space or tab. There is a space and a tab character within the square brackets. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; ^[    ]* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; indicates zero or more spaces or tabs at the start of a line. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; ^[    ]*Chapter &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; indicates the word *Chapter* on the left marginthat is, it can be indented and still match the pattern. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; The preceding sed command will replace the word *Chapter* with *Section* but only if *Chapter* is the first word on the line, ignoring any leading spaces. The replacement word *Section* will not be indented even if *Chapter* was indented. We will see in the next section how to preserve what wildcards matched, which would allow the replacement to have the same indentation. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Your command will still work if you include the g flag with the circumflex (^) or dollar sign ($) R.E. wildcards. The g flag is just unnecessary and slightly inefficient because there cannot be more than one match per line when you use either of these two R.E. wildcards. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; *Changing the Delimiter (*sed*)* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; The character immediately following &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; sed 's  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
|  

&#124; Page 417 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; is the delimiter that marks the start and end of the search pattern and replacement string. Slash (/), colon (:), and percent sign (%) are the most commonly used delimiters. These three commands all do the same thing: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; sed 's/xxx/yyy/g' report7    # delimiter is slash (/) sed 's:xxx:yyy:g' report7    # delimiter is colon (:)
sed 's%xxx%yyy%g' report7    # delimiter is percent sign (%) &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Choose a delimiter that is not a character in the search pattern or the replacement string. To change all occurrences of /usr/fred to /usr/jane, for example, I would choose a delimiter other than slash (/). For example: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; sed 's:/usr/fred:/usr/jane:g' report7 &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Some UNIX systems freely allow any character to be used as the delimiter besides the three common ones that I have mentioned. Alternatively you can put a backslash (\) before the delimiter character to use it within the source or destination string if you dont want to change the delimiter. The following line is equivalent to the preceding example, but more difficult to read: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; sed 's/\/usr\/fred/\/usr\/jane/g' report7 &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; *Removing (Deleting) a String from a Line (*sed, R.E.*)* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; To remove or delete a string, use the sed replacement command and specify an empty replacement string. For example: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; sed 's/ (LPX)//g' report &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; This example searches for a space followed by LPX in parentheses and will delete those six characters wherever found. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; *Selective Replacement or Deletion* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; We can limit which lines sed acts on to do replacement or deletion. One way to do that is to specify a starting and ending line number. For example: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; sed '14,253 s/Mr. Smith/Ms. Wilson/g' report7 &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 14 &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; specifies the starting line number for sed to start making replacements. Line 1 is the first line of the file or pipeline. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 253 &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; specifies the last line number for sed replacements. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;

 &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
|  

&#124; Page 418 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Use a dollar sign ($) to specify the last line of the file, as follows: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; sed '14,$ s/Mr. Smith/Ms. Wilson/g' report7 &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; This command is useful when you want to process most of a file, but it has a header section that you dont want to process. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Another way to selectively replace or delete a pattern is to specify a qualifying pattern that must appear on the lines to be processed. For example: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; sed '/Acme/ s/Mr. Smith/Ms. Wilson/g' report7 &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; In the preceding example, the replacement will only occur on lines that contain the qualifying string Acme. Instead of Acme, we could also have specified a qualifying pattern containing R.E. wildcards. If the qualifying pattern contains a slash (/), precede it with a backslash (\), as follows: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; sed '/\/usr\/fred/ s/Mr. Smith/Ms. Wilson/g' report7 &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; In this example, the replacement will only occur on lines that contain the qualifying string /usr/fred. You can also use an initial \x to select any character *x* as the delimiter for the qualifying pattern. For example: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; sed '\:/usr/fred: s/Mr. Smith/Ms. Wilson/g' report7 &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; In the preceding example, the replacement will only occur on lines that contain the qualifying string /usr/fred. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; If you want to process a section of consecutive lines but dont know the starting and ending line number, you can use patterns to specify start and end, as follows: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; sed '/^ *Chapter 2/,/^ *Chapter 3/ s/Mr. Smith/Ms. Wilson/g' ![arrow.gif](content/4505ed21b36efb4ebf4df5206fc03bad.gif)report7 &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; In this example, the replacement will occur on all output lines in the section of report7 whose first line has the words *Chapter 2,* which may come after some leading spaces. The section for replacement ends on the line that contains *Chapter 3* (again leading spaces are allowed). Notice both patterns are in slashes (/) and separated by a comma (,). &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
|  

&#124; Page 419 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; *Using Special Characters* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; To search for a literal asterisk (*) or period (.) in the search pattern, precede that character with a backslash (\) so that sed will not take it as a wildcard. For example: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; sed 's/321\.43/421.43/g' report7 &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; In the preceding example, the backslash (\) indicates that the following period is not a wildcard, so sed will search for 321.43 and replace all occurrences of that exact string with 421.43. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; There is no way to search for a pattern that begins on one line and ends on the next line. You cannot use \n in either the search pattern or the replacement string. You can use an escaped newline to start a newline in the replacement string, as follows: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; $ date &#124; sed 's/ /\ >/g'
Sun
Mar
22
11:38:09
PST
1998
$ &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; In this example, you are changing each space in the output to a newline. Notice we put a backslash before pressing the Enter key for the newline in the sed replacement string. We then get our PS2 prompt (>), which tells us we are still entering part of a previous command. We then enter the rest of the sed command. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; To include a literal single quotation mark (') in either the search or replacement strings, you cannot use single quotation marks to enclose the strings as in previous examples. Also using a preceding backslash to quote the internal single quotation mark (') does not help. You must change to double quotation marks around the sed command, as follows: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; sed "s/it's/it is/g" report7 &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; See the following section for other issues when using sed with double quotation marks rather than single quotation marks. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
|  

&#124; Page 420 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; *Using Shell Variables in the Search or Replacement String* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; If there is a phrase that you use often in the search or replacement string, you can save it in a shell variable for easy re-use, as follows: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; CO="Acme" &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; To use shell variables in your sed command, use double quotation marks rather than single quotation marks, as follows: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; sed "s/president of $CO/chairman of $CO/g" report7 &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; This command searches for president of Acme and changes those words to chairman of Acme. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; If a shell variable is adjacent to other letters or digits or underscore, enclose the variable in curly braces {}, as follows: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; sed "s/president of ${CO}Ltd/chairman of ${CO}Ltd/g" report7 &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; The preceding command searches for president of AcmeLtd and change those words to chairman of AcmeLtd. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; When using double quotation marks rather than single quotation marks, you must also put a backslash (\) before the following: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; A dollar sign ($), if not beginning a shell variable &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; A backquote (`), if not enclosing command substitution &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; A double quotation mark inside your string &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; You must also change any literal backslashes (\) in your search or replacement string into four backslashes (\). (This is because the shell will remove two of them, and the backslash must be preceded by a backslash to indicate a literal backslash.) &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; SEE ALSO &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; ![sarrow.gif](content/ad91af06ad96c57f0a338bded4c42f0e.gif)*For more information on shell variables see page 30* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
|  

&#124; Page 421 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; *Don't Replace 0 or More Occurrences (*sed*)* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Assume that report7 contains these lines: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; five trucks XXX three XX cars &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Assume that we want to replace any group of Xs with a question mark (?). Here is the wrong way to do that: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; sed 's/X*/?/g' report7           # wrong way &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Here is the output from the preceding command: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; ?f?i?v?e? ?t?r?u?c?k?s? ?? ?t?h?r?e?e? ?? ?c?a?r?s? &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; The reason we see the replacement string so many times is because there are always zero occurrences of any character between any two other characters. If I have the letters *ab,* for example, there are zero occurrences of the letter *X* between those two characters. To correct the preceding sed command, we should specify one or more *X*s, not zero or more *X*s. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Here is the correct sed command to use: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; sed 's/XX*/?/g' report7           # correct way &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; XX* specifies one *X* followed by zero or more *X*s, which is equivalent to one or more *X*s. Here is the output from that command: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; five trucks ? three ? cars &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; *Using, in the Replacement String, What a Wildcard Matched (*sed*).* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; If you enclose part or all of the R.E. pattern in escaped parentheses, sed will remember the exact characters that matched that part of the pattern. You can then use the remembered string in the replacement pattern as \1. Use \2 for a second remembered pattern, and so on. Here is an example we analyzed previously in this chapter: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; sed 's/^[    ]*Chapter/Section/' book3 &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
|  

&#124; Page 422 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; It changes *Chapter* to *Section* but, as we saw, the replacement string loses the left margin it had previously. We can correct that as follows: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; sed 's/^\([    ]*\)Chapter/\1Section/' book3 &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; \(  \) &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; are the escaped parentheses. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; \([    ]*\)  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; uses escaped parentheses to remember how many spaces or tabs were found at the left margin before the word *Chapter*. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
