Pressing Ctrl+V causes vi to display a circumflex (^) to alert you that the very next character input, if it is a control character, will be treated as just another data character in the line. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Now you are ready to actually set up a mapping. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; How to Map a Key to a Sequence of Commands &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 1\. From vis Command mode (that is, not Insert mode), enter a colon (:). The cursor should go down to the last line on the screen and a colon (:) prompt will appear there. Do not press Enter until instructed. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 2\. In the preceding procedure, you determined whether your terminal supports Ctrl+V in Visual mode. If your terminal does not support Ctrl+V in Visual mode (or if you are not sure), from vi Command mode enter Q. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Notice that this is a capital *Q*. Do not press Enter. The cursor will go to the bottom of the screen and a colon (:) prompt will appear. You have now left Visual mode. This step is not needed, but is harmless if your terminal does support Ctrl+V in Visual mode. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 3\. Enter map. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Do not press Enter until instructed. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 4\. Enter a space, and then enter the desired command letter to map. You should avoid any letter that is a vi command because you will not be able to do that command any more after that letter is mapped. Actually only five upper- or lowercase letters are not vi commands: *g K q v V*. I usually map &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
|  

&#124; Page 478 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; *g* to format paragraphs, as shown in the preceding chapter. I recommend against mapping capital *K* because *h,* *j,* *k,* and *l* are used to move the cursor, and we dont want usage of those cursor motion letters disturbing our text if the Caps Lock has been accidentally left on. Therefore I recommend that you use lowercase *v* or uppercase *V* as the desired command letter to map. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 5\. Enter a space, and then enter the vi command sequence to enter every time the mapped letter is pressed. As you saw earlier, enter a Ctrl+V before any control characters or Esc or the Enter key in your command sequence. The Ctrl+V will cause a circumflex (^) to appear before your control character. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 6\. Now press Enter to complete your map command. Because you did not precede it with a Ctrl+V, this Enter key terminates the map command. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 7\. If your terminal does not support Ctrl+V, you will still be on the last line with a colon (:) prompt. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Enter vi, and then press Enter. This returns you to Visual mode. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 8\. Your cursor should now have left the bottom line and you are in vi Command mode ready to enter vi commands, including the new command letter that you just mapped. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; When you have hundreds of repetitive editing changes to make, the best way to speed this up is to set up two-finger editingas discussed earlierusing the n command to search for the next pattern to change and the period (.) command to repeat the last change. If the last change is too complicated to be done by a single command, set up a mapping so that the whole command sequence can be done by a single letter like the *v* key. Use the slash (/) command to find the first occurrence to change. Now put one index finger on the *n* key and the other index finger on the *v* key. Press *n* to find the next occurrence to change. Press *v* only if you want to change it. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; You will lose your mapping when you exit from vi. In the preceding chapter on vi, in the section on formatting paragraphs, &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
|  

&#124; Page 479 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; you saw how to put the letter *g* mapping into a file called .exrc in your home directory. Notice that in this file, you put the complete map command but you do not put a colon (:) before the word *map*. Any mapping set up in .exrc in your home directory is available to you every time you use vi. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; *Preventing* J *from Turning Your Text to Mush.* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; If you use h, j, k, and l to move the cursor instead of the arrow keys, you will discover that, if the Caps Lock is accidentally on, it is harmless to enter H, K, and L: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; H moves the cursor to the highest line on the screen. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; K is not a command (as long you dont map this character). &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; L moves the cursor to the lowest line on the screen. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;  &#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Why is Ctrl+V a problem on some terminals? &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;  &#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; If your TERM is set to tvi925, a down-arrow sends a Ctrl+V. If you press Ctrl+V while in vi on that terminal, vi will think that a down-arrow key has been pressed, so vi gets confused. We can eliminate the problem by using *Q* to exit from Visual mode temporarily. Alternatively you will not have problems with Ctrl+V if you set your TERM to vt100 or ANSI. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; If you wanted to go down 10 lines and so pressed the j key 10 times, but did not notice that your Caps Lock was on, you would now find that you have joined 10 lines together. You will have created one long line that probably takes up more than one line and it looks like mush. To fix it, you must painstakingly insert the missing Enter key at the end of each of the original lines. The J command also trims any leading spaces in the line, so you would have to re-enter any leading spaces. After you have made this mistake a couple of times, you may wish there was a way to prevent this problem. There is, and I will show you how I do it. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Preventing problems with accidental Js &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 1\. Put this mapping in your .exrc file in your home directory: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; map J J: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 2\. Having done that, if you enter several capital *J*s by mistake, the first *J* will join two lines and then go into Colon (:) mode on the bottom line. The rest of the *J*s will harmlessly appear on the bottom line. After you realize your mistake, just press Backspace or Ctrl+H until you have moved all the way to the left and are off the last line. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 3\. Enter u if you want to undo the effect of the single J command that was executed. You have now fully recovered from your mistake. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
|  

&#124; Page 480 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; If you do want to join several lines together, you can still do so by preceding the *J* with a repeat count. This will join the requested number of lines and then go into Colon mode on the bottom line. Just press Backspace or Esc to leave the bottom line and continue your other editing. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;  &#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Dont map the K key &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;  &#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Of the four cursor motion commands: h, j, k, and l, only j is a problem if the Caps Lock is accidentally left on. If you map the *K* key, however, you could have two problem keys. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Global and Partial Text Substitution &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; vi has a built-in colon command g to globally search for and replace all occurrences of one pattern with another. Because you just learned how to use sed and awk in the previous chapters, however, I am going to show you how to use other UNIX commands, like sed and awk, to modify your whole file or any part of your file. After you learn this technique, you can do much more than the global g command can do. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; *Substituting R.E. Patterns Throughout the File* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; How to Globally Replace a Pattern in Your Document &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 1\. In vi Command mode, enter a colon (:). This should move the cursor to the last line where a colon prompt is waiting. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 2\. Enter the following: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; %! sed 's/R.E./newstring/g' %! tells vi to apply the following UNIX command to all
lines of your file.
sed is the stream editor that we looked at in a previous
chapter.
s is the sed command to substitute one string for another.
R.E. stands for regular expression.  Enter the string to
search for which may include R.E. wildcards.
newstring stands for the replacement string to be put
wherever the R.E. string is found.
g tells sed to do this substitution as many times as the
source string is found.  You may leave off the g to tell
sed to only
    replace the first occurrence of the source string on
    ![arrow.gif](content/4505ed21b36efb4ebf4df5206fc03bad.gif)any line but
    not subsequent occurrences on the same line. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
|  

&#124; Page 481 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 3\. Press Enter to execute your command. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 4\. The changes will be made to all lines and you should now be back in vi Command mode. On some types of UNIX systems, you may be prompted to press Enter or Return to continue. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 5\. Check the lines of your file to see whether you are happy with the changes made. If not, you can remove all the changes by entering the u command to undo them. Remember the u command can only undo the preceding change, so check the file immediately after doing these replacements. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; SEE ALSO &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; ![sarrow.gif](content/ad91af06ad96c57f0a338bded4c42f0e.gif)*For more information on R.E. patterns, see page 388* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; *Substituting R.E. Patterns in a Portion of the File* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Using the technique in the preceding section, you can also do the replacement only in a section of the file (which is not possible with the global g command that was not covered). The following procedure uses the fact that you can set marks in the file to reference that line, as you saw in an earlier chapter on vi. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;  &#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Why not use built-in vi replacement commands? &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;  &#124; ![fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif](content/fc4f3a8aef38b56941e55505c60e4caf.gif) &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; vi supports two built-in colon commands, g (global) and s (substitution, which I dont cover in this book because calling the external sed command fills the same function as both of these built-in commands. This gives you more practice with sed, which is an important UNIX command and shows you how to call other external UNIX commands to manipulate your text (as you shall see). &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; How to substitute strings in a section of the file &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 1\. In vi, move the cursor to the start of the section where the text substitution is desired. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 2\. Enter ma. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; This will set mark a at that line. If mark a is already in use to mark another line of the file, you can choose any other letter for your mark. You can have up to 26 marks set. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 3\. Move the cursor to the last line of the section to be modified. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 4\. Enter !'a. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Do not press the Enter key until instructed. Change the letter *a* in the preceding example if you are using a different mark. Notice that the quotation mark is a single quotation &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
|  

&#124; Page 482 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; mark, not a backquote. This should take the cursor to the last line and a bang sign (!) prompt should appear there. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 5\. Enter the following: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; sed 's/R.E./newstring/g' &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; This is the same sed command that we analyzed in the preceding step-by-step procedure. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 6\. Press Enter to execute your command. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 7\. The changes will be made to the section of your file and you should now be back in vi Command mode. On some types of UNIX systems, you may be prompted to press Enter or Return to continue. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Check the lines of your file to see whether you are happy with the changes made. If not, you can remove all the changes by entering the u command to undo them. Remember the u command can only undo the preceding change, so check the file immediately after doing these replacements. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; To summarize: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;    :%! sed ...   replaces throughout the file    !'a sed ...   replaces back to or forward to mark a &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; SEE ALSO &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; ![sarrow.gif](content/ad91af06ad96c57f0a338bded4c42f0e.gif)*For more information on setting marks in vi, see page 467* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; *Conditionally Substituting Text in vi.* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; We can replace the sed command in the preceding section with other sed commands or other different commands entirely to give us great control over how text is substituted in vi. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; :%! sed '/R.E.1/ s/R.E.2/newstring/g'         # general ![arrow.gif](content/4505ed21b36efb4ebf4df5206fc03bad.gif)form
:%! sed '/acme$/ s/^president/chairperson/g'   # example &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; The first line shows the general form of a modified sed command that we can also use in vi to conditionally substitute text. In this form of the sed command, sed will search for R.E.2 and replace it with newstring, but only in lines that contain R.E.1. In the second line, you can see an example using this form of sed. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
|  

&#124; Page 483 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; In that example, if president occurs at the start of a line, we will replace it with chairperson, but only if the line ends in the word acme. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; :%! awk '$n == "sstring" {gsub("R.E.2","newstring")} ![arrow.gif](content/4505ed21b36efb4ebf4df5206fc03bad.gif){print}' # general form
:%! awk '$3 == "K6697" {gsub("D...","M46253")} {print}'
![arrow.gif](content/4505ed21b36efb4ebf4df5206fc03bad.gif)# example &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; The first line shows the general form of an awk command that we can also use in vi to conditionally substitute text. Using awk, we can check a particular field to decide whether we should do the text substitution in that line. In this form of the awk command, awk searches for all occurrences of R.E.2 and replaces them with newstring, but only in lines where field n exactly matches sstring. In the second line, you can see an example using this form of awk. In that example, any time that D is followed by three characters, the D and those three characters will be replaced with M46253, but only if field 3 of the line contains K6697. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; :%! awk '$n >= numval {gsub("R.E.2","newstring")} {print}' # ![arrow.gif](content/4505ed21b36efb4ebf4df5206fc03bad.gif)general form
:%! awk '$3 >= 16.2 {gsub("D...","M46253")} {print}'       #
![arrow.gif](content/4505ed21b36efb4ebf4df5206fc03bad.gif)example &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; This example shows the general form and an example which is similar to the preceding awk command. Use this awk form when you want to do a substitution, but only if a particular field contains a value greater than or equal to numval. We can replace >= with the following: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;    >=  (greater than or equal)    <=  (less than or equal)
   ==  (equal to)
   !=  (not equal to)
   >   (greater than)
   <   (less than)
:%! awk '$n ~ /R.E.1/ {gsub("R.E.2","newstring")} {print}' #
![arrow.gif](content/4505ed21b36efb4ebf4df5206fc03bad.gif)general form
:%! awk '$3 ~ /P[0-9]$/ {gsub("D...","M46253")} {print}'   #
![arrow.gif](content/4505ed21b36efb4ebf4df5206fc03bad.gif)example &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; The preceding example again shows the general form and an example that is similar to the two previous awk commands. Use &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
|  

&#124; Page 484 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; the preceding awk form when you want to do a substitution, but only if a particular field contains an R.E. pattern. In the specific example here, any time that D is followed by three characters, the D and those three characters will be replaced with M46253, but only if field 3 of the line ends with a P followed by a digit. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; *Changing the Indentation of Your Lines* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; You can change the indentation by using the sed command to either add spaces to the left margin or remove them. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; :%! sed 's/^ *//' &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; The preceding sed command removes all leading spaces for all lines of the file. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; !'a sed 's/^ *//' &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; This sed command removes all leading spaces from the current line to mark a. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; :%! sed 's/^/   /' &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; The preceding sed command adds three leading spaces to each line of the file. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; !'a sed 's/^/   /' &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; This sed command adds three leading spaces to the lines starting from the current line to mark a. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Moving/Copying Sections of Text in vi &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Moving and copying sections of text can by done in several ways. I will show you how to use marks to do this because I think it gives you the best control and the most successful results. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
|  

&#124; Page 485 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; *Moving/Copying Text in the Same File* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Moving/copying Text in the Same File &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 1\. In vi, move the cursor to the start of the text to move or copy. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 2\. Enter ma. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; This command executes without pressing Enter. It sets mark a at that line. If mark a is already in use to mark another line of the file, you can choose any other letter for your mark. You can have up to 26 marks set. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 3\. Move the cursor to the last line of the section to be moved or copied. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 4\. To move the text, enter d'a. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; This command executes without pressing Enter. It deletes all text from the current line to and including mark a, and saves it in what is called an unnamed buffer. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 5\. To copy the text, enter y'a. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; This command executes without pressing Enter. It yanksthat is, copiesall text from the current line to and including mark a and saves it in what is called an unnamed buffer. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 6\. Move the cursor to the line just above the desired place to put the moved or copied text. If you want to move or copy text to the beginning of the file, you must insert a blank line at the start of the file, so you can be in the line just above where you want to do the insert. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 7\. Enter p. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; This command executes without pressing Enter. It will pastethat is, insertall text saved in the unnamed buffer by the previous steps 4 or 5. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; *Moving/Copying Text Between Different Files* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Moving/Copying Text Between Different Files &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 1\. Use vi to edit the source filethat is, the file that contains the text to be moved or copied. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
|  

&#124; Page 486 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 2\. Move the cursor to the start of the text to move or copy. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 3\. Enter ma. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; This command executes without pressing Enter. It sets mark a at that line. If mark a is already in use to mark another line of the file, you can choose any other letter for your mark. You can have up to 26 marks set. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 4\. Move the cursor to the last line of the section to be moved or copied. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 5\. To move the text, enter "bd'a. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; This command executes without pressing Enter. It deletes all text from the current line to and including mark a and saves it in buffer b. If buffer b is already in use saving other text, you can choose any other letter for your buffer. You can save text in up to 26 buffers, named for each letter of the alphabet and hence they are also called named buffers. Named buffers are always preceded by double quotation marks (). The letter of mark used and the letter of the named buffer do not have to be the same. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 6\. To copy the text, enter "by'a. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; This command executes without pressing Enter. It yanksthat is, copiesall text from the current line to and including mark a and saves it in buffer b. If buffer b is already in use saving other text, you can choose any other letter for your buffer. You can save text in up to 26 buffers, named for each letter of the alphabet and hence called named buffers. Named buffers are always preceded by double quotation marks (). The letter of mark used and the letter of the named buffer do not have to be the same. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 7\. If you have done any text modifications in this file that you want to preserve, save your changes now. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Enter :w. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; The preceding vi command writes the vi workspace to the file. Do not exit from vi at this point because that would clear all of vis unnamed and named buffers. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 8\. Enter :e file2. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
|  

&#124; Page 487 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Colon (:) e changes the file you are editing while preserving the text in named buffers. Replace file2 in the preceding command with the name of the file to which you want to move or copy the saved text. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 9\. In this new file, move the cursor to the line just above the desired place in this file to put the moved or copied text. If you want to move or copy text to the beginning of this file, you must insert a blank line at the start of the file, so you can be in the line just above where you want to do the insert. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 10\. Enter "bp. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; This command executes without pressing Enter. It pastesthat is, insertsall text saved in the buffer b by the previous steps 5 or 6. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Setting Options for Inserting Text. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; In vi, the set command enables you to turn on or off various modes in vi. This section looks at modes that enhance text input. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; *Setting vi to Always Show the Input Mode* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Sometimes people have trouble in vi because they lose track of whether they are in Insert mode or Command mode. I have seen files created by beginners that contain lines like this: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; :wq :w!q
:wq!
wq
q
:q &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; vi has a mode that tells you in the bottom right-hand corner of the screen if you are in Insert mode, Replace mode, Append mode, and so on. To turn on this mode, enter the following: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; :set showmode &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
|  

&#124; Page 488 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; To turn off this mode, enter this: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; :set noshowmode &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; *Turning on Autowrap at End of Line* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; vi has a mode that will check whether you are near the end of line when inserting text. If so, it takes the current word and moves it to the start of the next line as though you had pressed the Enter key just before the start of this word. With this mode on, you never have to press Enter. vi autowraps the line for you. To turn this mode on, enter the following: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; :set wrapmargin=10 &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; The preceding command causes any word that gets within 10 characters of the end of the line to autowrap to the start of the next line. You can set a larger or smaller number than 10 to determine where you want to wrap the end of line. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; To turn off this mode, enter this: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; :set wrapmargin=0 &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; This command may be abbreviated as wm, as follows: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; :set wm=10 &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; *Turning on Autoindent at Start of Line* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; If you are using vi in a document with an indented left margin, it will be useful for you to turn on Autoindent mode. Anytime you advance to the next line while in Insert, Append, or Replace mode, vi automatically enters the same number of spaces as on the preceding line. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; To turn off this mode, enter the following: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; :set noautoindent &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; You can abbreviate this command as ai, as follows: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; :set ai :set noai &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
|  

&#124; Page 489 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; *Using Abbreviations for Long Strings* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; If you have a long phrase to enter frequently, you can set up an input abbreviation that vi will expand for you as soon as you insert the abbreviation. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Setting Up and Using vi Abbreviations &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 1\. In vi, enter colon (:), and then enter abbrev. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Do not press Enter until instructed. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 2\. Enter a space, and then enter the abbreviation you want to use to signal that the long phrase is really to be inserted at the cursor. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 3\. Enter a space, and then enter the long phrase itself. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 4\. Press Enter to set up this abbreviation. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 5\. To make use of the abbreviation that has been set up, from vi, go into Insert mode and start inserting text. As part of the text you enter, insert the abbreviation from step 2\. You should see that the abbreviation text is immediately expanded by vi to the longer phrase. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; *Number Lines* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; In vi, there is a mode to show line numbers before each line of a file. These line numbers are not inserted into the file itself, but are just displayed to the screen. This can be useful if you compile a C language program and the compiler tells you that you have an error at line 1453. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; To turn on vi line numbering, enter the following: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; :set number &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; To turn off this mode, enter this: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; :set nonumber &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; This command can be abbreviated as nu, as follows: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; :set nu :set nonu &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
|  

&#124; Page 490 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; *Ignoring Case When Searching Using/or?* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; To ignore case when searching ahead for strings using slash (/) or searching backward using question mark (?), enter the following: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; :set ignorecase &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; To turn off this mode, enter this: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; :set noignorecase &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; You can abbreviate this command as ic, as follows: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; :set ic :set noic &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; *Saving Your Options in .exrc* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; If you have :set options that you want to use every time you enter vi, you can create a file called .exrc in your home directory. It can contain set options, map commands, and abbreviations, as follows: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; set autoindent set ignorecase
set showmode
set wm=10
map g 072lBi^M^[
map J J:
abbrev SVR4 UNIX, System V, Release 4 &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Notice that each line in this file does *not* start with a colon (:). &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; SEE ALSO &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; ![sarrow.gif](content/ad91af06ad96c57f0a338bded4c42f0e.gif)*For more information on home directories, see page 44* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Harnessing Other UNIX Commands to Work in vi &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Earlier you saw how to apply sed to some or all of the lines of the file. You can use that same technique to use other UNIX commands to manipulate lines in vi. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
|  

&#124; Page 491 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; *Checking Other UNIX Commands While in vi* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; While you are editing in vi, you might want to look up some information by running other UNIX commands or pipelines. You can do this from vi Command mode, by entering this: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; :! cmd &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Replace cmd in the preceding command with the desired UNIX command or pipeline you want to run. The output from that command will appear on your screen. At the end, it will prompt you to press the Enter key. Then you will be back in vi Command mode ready to do more editing of your file. You saw this process in the preceding chapter on vi when you wrote a script that displayed a help message for vi. In that exercise, we used the colon bang (:!) to run the vihelp script so that we could see the help message and then resume editing. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; :! cal 1998 &#124; pg &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; The preceding example displays a calendar of the year 1998, one page at a time. You can now use pg to go back and forth in the calendar for 1998 to look up what day a particular date falls on. After you end this cal 1998 pipeline, you will automatically resume your editing in vi with the current screen completely refreshed. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; *Inserting the Output of Other UNIX Commands into Your File* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; You can insert the output from any UNIX command or pipeline into your file by moving the cursor to a blank line. Then enter this: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; !! cmd &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Replace cmd in the preceding command with the desired UNIX command or pipeline you want to run. Bang-bang (!!) causes the current line you are on to be provided as standard input to the cmd you enter. The output from that command will be inserted in your file in place of the current line. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
|  

&#124; Page 492 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; !! cal 1999 &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; This example inserts a calendar of the year 1999 into your file in place of the current line. Hint: I usually enter this type of command on a blank line. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; !! cat ffile &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; The preceding vi command inserts the contents of ffile in place of the current line. ffile can be specified as a basename, or as an absolute or relative pathname. Alternatively, you can use the built-in vi command :r ffile to insert the contents of ffile at the current cursor position. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; *Sorting All or Part of the File* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; In vi, you can sort all the lines of your file by entering the following: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; :%! sort &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; You can enter any desired sort options (see Appendix A). All lines of the file will be passed to the sort command. The output of the sort command will replace the current contents of the file. If you dont like the results, you can enter u to undo that last modification. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; How to Sort a Section of Your File &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 1\. Move the cursor to the start of the section to sort. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 2\. Enter ma. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; This command executes without pressing Enter. It sets mark a at that line. If mark a is already in use to mark another line of the file, you can choose any other letter for your mark. You can have up to 26 marks set. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 3\. Move the cursor to the last line of the section to be sorted. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 4\. Enter !'a sort. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Enter any desired options after sort (see Appendix A). Press the Enter key to execute this command. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 5\. Now the lines in the section will be sorted. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; SEE ALSO &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; ![sarrow.gif](content/ad91af06ad96c57f0a338bded4c42f0e.gif)*For more information on the* sort *command, see page 202* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
|  

&#124; Page 493 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; *Deleting Lines That Match a Pattern* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; In vi, you can delete all the lines of your file that contain an R.E. pattern by entering the following: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; :%! grep -v 'R.E.' &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; You can enter any desired grep options (see Appendix A). All lines of the file will be passed to the grep command. The output of the grep command will replace the current contents of the file. If you dont like the results, you can enter u to undo that last modification. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Deleting Lines with a Pattern from a Section. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 1\. Move the cursor to the start of the section where you want to delete lines that contain a pattern. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 2\. Enter ma. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; This command executes without pressing Enter. It sets mark a at that line. If mark a is already in use to mark another line of the file, you can choose any other letter for your mark. You can have up to 26 marks set. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 3\. Move the cursor to the last line of the section. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 4\. Enter !'a grep -v R.E.. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Enter any desired options after grep (see Appendix A). Follow the standard rules for grep, including any needed quotation marks around the R.E. pattern. Press Enter to execute this command. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 5\. Now the lines in the section that contain the R.E. pattern will be removed. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; SEE ALSO &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; ![sarrow.gif](content/ad91af06ad96c57f0a338bded4c42f0e.gif)*For more information on the* grep *command, see page 380* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; *Encrypting/Decrypting All or Part of Your File* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; If your UNIX system supports the crypt command, you can apply the technique in the preceding section to crypt also. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; :%! crypt &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
|  

&#124; Page 494 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; The preceding vi command will ask you for a key. It will then use that key to encrypt or decrypt the whole file. Safeguard your key carefully because you cannot decrypt the text without it. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; !'a crypt &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; The preceding vi command will encrypt or decrypt a section of the file from the current line to mark a. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; SEE ALSO &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; ![sarrow.gif](content/ad91af06ad96c57f0a338bded4c42f0e.gif)*For more information on the* crypt *command, see page 217* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; *Inserting a Banner Headline into Your Document* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; You can use the UNIX banner command to change a line so that each character is about 10 characters tall, as follows: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; !! banner &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; This vi command pipes the current line of the file to banner and replaces that line with the output from banner. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; SEE ALSO &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; ![sarrow.gif](content/ad91af06ad96c57f0a338bded4c42f0e.gif)*For more information on the* banner *command, see page 167* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; *Printing a Section of Your File* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Printing a section of your file from vi &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 1\. In vi Command mode, enter the following: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; :w &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; This vi command writes the file to disk, which is important to do before the rest of these steps. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 2\. Set mark a at the start of the section to print. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 3\. Move to the end of the section to print and enter: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; !'a lp &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; You can use either lp or lpr, depending on which one your system supports. You can add any desired options, such as selecting the destination printer or number of copies. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 4\. The preceding command deletes all the lines to be printed from your file. Enter u to undo the deletion and restore those lines to your file. It is very important that the u command be run immediately after step 3. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
|  

&#124; Page 495 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; SEE ALSO &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; ![sarrow.gif](content/ad91af06ad96c57f0a338bded4c42f0e.gif)*For more information on printing, see page 169* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; *Counting Number of Lines/Words/Characters in Part of Your File* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Printing a section of your file from vi &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 1\. In vi Command mode, enter the following: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; :w &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; This vi command writes the file to disk, which is important to do before the rest of these steps. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 2\. Set mark a at the start of the section to be counted, as follows: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; ma &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 3\. Move to the end of the section to be counted, and enter this: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; !'a wc &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 4\. The preceding command deletes all the lines to be counted and replaces them with three numbers: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Number of lines in that section Number of words in that section
Number of characters in that section
Write down any of these numbers if you need them. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 5\. Enter u to undo the deletion and restore those lines to your file. It is very important that the u command be run immediately after step 3. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; *Editing Multiple Files* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; You can give vi a list of files to edit, as follows: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; vi report* &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; When you finish editing one file, save it (:w) and use :n to start editing the next file in the list. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
|  

&#124; Page 497 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Chapter 19 Command-Line Editing in the Korn Shell &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; By Sanjiv Guha &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Invoking Command-Line Edit Options &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; History of Commands &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; *vi* COMMAND EDIT MODE &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Alias &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
|  

&#124; Page 498 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; While working with UNIX or, for that matter, any other operating system, you must correct key entry errors by using the available keys on the terminal. However, not all keyboards have the same layout and, furthermore, may not have the same keys. Because of this, you may not be able to correct keying errors and may find yourself retyping whole command strings. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; *Korn shell* provides two different ways of editing commands in the command line. You can either use keys used by the source editor vi or you can use the source editor emacs. Depending on which editor you are familiar with, you can invoke either of these options for command line editing. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; You must explicitly invoke either the vi or emacs command-line editing option. If you do not do so in your .profile file, then by default you get the Korn Shell line-editing options, which are minimal. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Invoking Command-Line Edit Options. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; If you are familiar with vi, then you can use the following command on the command line or have it in the .profile file (which gets executed at logon) to use vi command for command-line editing: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; set -o vi &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; On the other hand, if you are familiar with emacs editor, use the following command: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; set -o emacs &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; You can have only one of these active at any time. The most recent command is in effect. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; History of Commands &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Korn shell keeps a history of the commands across the session. That is, even if you log out, you can still obtain the commands you entered in the previous session by using the Korn shell command fc. The history is, by default, stored in the &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
|  

&#124; Page 499 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; $HOME/.sh_history file, where $HOME is the home directory for the user. If you want to modify the filename for the history file, you can modify the filename specified in the system variable HISTFILE. You can include the following command in the .profile file to modify the history file name. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; export HISTFILE=$HOME/myhistoryfile &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; If you want to get a list of the last few commands, enter the following: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; fc -l &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; The system responds as follows: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 116  ls -l 117  ls
118  find . -print
119  vi test.c
120  rm test.c &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; The numbers on the left are the line numbers of the commands in the history file. A higher number indicates a more recent command than one with a lower number. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; If you want to obtain a list of commands within a specified number of lines, use the following command: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; fc -l 117 119 &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; This command lists the command numbers 117 through 119 in the history file: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 117  ls 118  find . -print
119  vi test.c &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; You can also use *relative number* to list the commands. The following command lists all commands starting with the second to last command from the most recent command: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; fc -l -2 &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; The system response is as follows: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 118  find . -print 119  vi test.c
120  rm test.c &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
|  

&#124; Page 500 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; If you want to obtain the list of commands in reverse order, you can use the following command: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; fc -l -r -2 &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; The system response is as follows: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; 117  rm test.c 118  vi test.c
118  find . -print &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; You can also execute just one of the commands in the history file using the -s flag with fc command. If you want to execute the most recent command only, use the following command: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; fc -s &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; If you want to execute the command at line 118, for example, you can use the following command: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; fc -s 118 &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; vi Command Edit Mode &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; The vi command-line editor, like the source editor, has two modes: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Entry mode &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Command mode &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; In the *entry mode,* you enter the command and press Enter to signal the entry of the command so that the command is executed. You can use the Esc key at any time while in entry mode to switch to command mode. In the command mode, you can navigate to any part of the command you have entered so far and modify it, including inserting new strings in the middle of the command. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; In the *command mode,* you can use one or more letters to activate different editing commands of vi. While in the command mode, if you press a key that does not translate to a vi command, then you usually hear a beep sound from the terminal. In vi command mode, lowercase letters have different meanings from the uppercase letters. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
|  

&#124; Page 501 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Korn shell keeps a history of the previous commands you have entered. You can use the command-line editing commands to recall these commands and modify or add to them before executing them. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Now take a look at some details of the command-line editing commands when set -o vi has been used to set vi as the command-line editor. The commands are discussed in alphabetic order: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; a &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Invokes insert mode so that text can be entered after the current cursor position. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; A &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Invokes insert mode so that text can be entered at the end of current line. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; b &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Allows cursor to move back one character at a time. You can prefix it with a number *n* to repeat it *n* times. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; B &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Allows cursor to be moved back to the previous word (blank, delimited text). You can prefix it with a number *n* to repeat it *n* times. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; C &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Deletes all the characters from the current position to end of the line and allows you to enter new characters. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; dd &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Deletes complete line of text. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; D &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Deletes to the end of the line from the current cursor position. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; e &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Moves the cursor to the end of the current word. You can prefix it with a number *n* to repeat it *n* times. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; E &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Moves the cursor to the end of the blank, delimited word. You can prefix it with a number *n* to repeat it *n* times. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;

 &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
|  

&#124; Page 502 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; f followed by a character &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Moves the cursor to the next occurrence of the specified character. You can prefix it with a number *n* to repeat it *n* times. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; F followed by a character &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Moves the cursor to the previous occurrence of the specified character. You can prefix it with a number *n* to repeat it *n* times. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; G &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Brings up the earliest command in the command history file. You can prefix it with a number *n* to position the command number *n* in the command history file. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; h &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Moves cursor to the left by one character. You can prefix it with a number *n* to repeat it *n* times. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; i &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Puts you in insert mode before the current position of the cursor to enter text. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; I &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Puts you in insert mode before the first non-blank character in the line. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; j &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Brings up the next command from the command history file. You can prefix it with a number *n* to repeat it *n* times. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; k &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Brings up the previous command from the command history file. You can prefix it with a number *n* to repeat it *n* times. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; l &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Moves cursor to the right by one character. You can prefix it with a number *n* to repeat it *n* times. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; n &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Repeats the last search of the command history file. The direction of the search is from most recent command to least recent command. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;

 &#124;

 |

|  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

 |
