&#124; Page 503 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; N &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Repeats the last search of the command history file. The direction of the search is from least recent command to most recent command. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; p &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Inserts the text from the delete or yank buffer after the cursor position. You can prefix it with a number *n* to repeat it *n* times. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; P &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Inserts the text from the delete or yank buffer before the cursor position. You can prefix it with a number *n* to repeat it *n* times. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; r followed by a character &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Replaces the character at the current cursor position by the specified character. You can prefix it with a number *n* to repeat it *n* times. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; R &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Puts you in replace mode, in which you can override all characters from the current cursor position. You can go past the current last character. You can end the replace mode by pressing the Esc key. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; S &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Deletes the command line and puts you in insert mode for entering text. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; t followed by a character &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Moves cursor to the next occurrence of the specified character on the current command line. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; T followed by a character &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Moves cursor to the previous occurrence of the specified character on the current command line. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; u &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Undoes the last change made to the command line. If you repeat the u command, you toggle between the changed version of the command line and the non-modified version of the command line. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;

 &#124;

&#124;

&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; U &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Restores the original text in the command line by undoing all modifications. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; v &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Puts you in vi editor with the content of the current command line. You can then use standard vi commands to edit it. On exiting vi with :wq, each line is executed as a command one after the other. You can prefix it with a number *n* to edit the line number *n* in the command history file. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; w &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Moves the cursor to the next word on the command line. You can prefix it with a number *n* to repeat it *n* times. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; W &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Moves the cursor to the next space-delimited word on the command line. You can prefix it with a number *n* to repeat it *n* times. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; x &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Deletes the character at the cursor position and keep it in the delete buffer. You can prefix it with a number *n* to repeat it *n* times. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;

 &#124;

 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;

 &#124;

 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;

&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; &#124; &#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124; Moves cursor to the first character in the command line. If you prefix it with a number *n,* the cursor moves to the character position *n* on the command line. &#124;  &#124;

 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; / followed by a string and ending with Enter key &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Searches the command (history file for the specified) string anywhere in the command in the direction from most recent command to the least recent command. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; / followed by ^ and a string, and ending with Enter key &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Searches the command history file for the specified string at the beginning of the command in the direction from most recent command to the least recent command. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; ? followed by a string and ending with Enter key &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Searches the command history file for the specified string anywhere in the command in the direction from least recent command to the most recent command. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; ? followed by ^ and a string, and ending with Enter key &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Searches the command history file for the specified string at the beginning of the command in the direction from least recent command to the most recent command. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; ~ &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Modifies a lowercase letter to an uppercase letter, or vice versa. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;

 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;

&#124; Page 506 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; # &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Inserts a pound sign (#) at the beginning of the command line and executes it so that it goes to the command history file. The command is not actually executed because the # sign in the beginning means that Korn shell treats it as a comment. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; = &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Displays the file name, which matches the current word. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; * &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Replaces the current word with a list file and directory names starting with names matching the current word. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Space &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Same as l. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Enter &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Executes the current command. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;
&#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Control key followed by the letter l &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;  

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Redraws the current line. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

 &#124;

 &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; Alias &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; You can use the alias command to define a shortcut for a command string. There are two types of aliases: regular alias and tracked alias. A *tracked* alias shows you the complete path of the command. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; You can use the alias command by itself to generate a list of all aliases set up in the current environment. If you use the -t command as follows then you will get a list of all tracked aliases: &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; alias -t &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; You can use the alias command to define an alias for a command or for a number of commands. In the following example, an alias is set up for ls command as ls command but with the -l option. &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; alias ls="ls -l"  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124;  &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124; By Jesper Pedersen &#124;  &#124;
&#124;  &#124;

&#124;  &#124; Carrying on with emacs &#124;  &#124;
